div.p: PROLOGUE
Peter the Galician begins his Book on Animals thus:
Of all the arts and sciences discovered by the wise men of this world, one stands out as foremost and nobler than the rest: the one that treats of animals.

For this art brings benefit not only to the care of the body but also to the good of the soul, since through knowledge of animals and their nature we can arrive at the praise and knowledge of God the creator.
For as it is read in the book of Genesis: And God created the great whales, and every living and moving creature that moves in the waters.
Hence we too, wishing to investigate this science diligently, propose to speak first of the lion, since among all animals it is the noblest and most royal.

Since, depending on the earth's position relative to the equator, to the sun's two tropics, to each pole of the eighth heaven, and to the poles, tropics, and equator of the other two planets, a varied tempering and lack of tempering arises differently in different lands, different animals are generated in them, as Aristotle said. Likewise the seasons differ, since in some regions there is summer when in others there is winter, spring, and autumn, and the beginnings, middles, and ends of these seasons - and their remaining parts - vary accordingly. Correspondingly, blood vessels dry out or grow moist, and languages and speech vary too, as Abonacer said. For this reason different names are imposed on different things, and in different places different animals are generated in different ways; hence the science of animals is difficult, since we are ignorant either of the animals themselves or of their names - for few are familiar to us, few are domestic, and what is known to men is comprised within a small number - and our understanding grasps things as if at twilight, through a kind of haze; and many kinds of animals are minute and escape us, not being perceptible to our dull senses.

For this reason, I, brother Peter the Galician, of the order of Friars Minor, first bishop of Cartagena, having read through Aristotle's book on animals in the Arabic language, translated it into Latin as a summary of the sense of this book.
And we have inserted a few explanatory remarks, drawing on the commentary and glosses that we found on this book.

And we have cut out much material, partly because it was repeated many times over, and partly because not all - or even many - of the animals discussed are found among us, and even where they are, their names are unknown both to the Arabs and to the Latins, from whom we learned and in whose languages we examined this book.
And in some places we have arranged the material differently from how it stood in the original.

For there is clearly an error of order in certain places, which is believed to have arisen either from the fault of those who translated it from Greek into Arabic, or from the disciples who took notes after Aristotle, or from those who arranged the little parchment sheets of Aristotle's books, which they found in his archives after his death.
And let whoever this translation comes into the hands of take note of our labor, and do us the kindness of their prayers, just as we have done him the kindness of our efforts.

And we say that this book is divided into two parts: the first, extending from the beginning up to the twelfth book, deals with animals according to the division of their limbs and their habits and behavior; the second, from the twelfth book to the end, gives the causes underlying their limbs and their composition.

The first part is further subdivided: in the first ten books it treats of the limbs of animals and their operations and behavior, while in the eleventh it treats of the dialectical rules necessary for the master of natural science.

This first part is subdivided further still: from the beginning up to the fifth book it treats of animals by distinguishing their limbs, and from the fifth book onward it treats of them according to their operations.

It is subdivided yet again: from the beginning up to that passage in the fourth book - 'And he said that the organs of the senses are not present in animals in a single manner' - it treats of the vital limbs; from that passage onward it treats of the sensory limbs.
And this first part is subdivided once more, since from the beginning up to the fourth book it treats of animals that have blood, and thereafter of animals that lack blood.

And the first part is subdivided yet again: in the first section, extending from the beginning up to the chapter 'Flesh, and what resembles it' in the third book, it treats of the solid, fixed, or hard limbs; in the second, of the soft ones.

And this first part is subdivided still further: in its first section, extending from the beginning up to the passage in the third book, 'And in the bodies of animals there are other limbs,' it treats of the limbs generated from seed; in the second, of the limbs generated from surplus nourishment. And the first of these is divided again: in its first part, extending up to the passage 'And he said: Since blood and the veins are the origins of the heart,' it treats of the organic or heterogeneous limbs, composed of dissimilar parts; in the second, it treats of the homogeneous limbs made of similar parts.

And the first of these is subdivided: in its first part, extending up to the third book, it treats of the limbs that serve the regimen of the individual's own life; in the second, of the limbs that serve propagation into another like itself.

This is subdivided once more: in its first part, extending from the beginning up to the passage in the first book, 'And it is fitting that we speak first of the limbs of man,' it sets out the division of animals according to their parts, habitat, motion, manner of life, and behavior, and the like, in a general way, as if by way of a preface. In the second part it treats of the external and internal limbs of man and of the brute animals, each considered separately.
On the differences among animals in general

Of the parts of animals' bodies, some are simple and homogeneous, such as flesh and sinew, while others are composite and heterogeneous, such as the head, hands, and feet. The heterogeneous parts are made up of homogeneous ones. Among the homogeneous parts, some are soft and moist in every respect, or as long as they remain in their natural state - such as flesh, blood and the watery part of blood, suet, fat, marrow, seed, bile, and milk; others are dry and hard, such as sinews, veins, hair, cartilage, hoof, horns, and bones. And among the heterogeneous parts, some are mere parts, others are limbs proper, such as the head, hands, and feet.

According to these limbs and parts, some animals are alike, others are not. Animals of one and the same most specific species are alike, and it is in this sense that a horse is said to resemble a horse, and a man a man - for just as there is agreement of the whole to the whole, so there is agreement of each part to its corresponding part.

Animals of subordinate species are unlike one another, as are those of the same most specific species when of different sexes. For some differ in respect of privation and possession, some in respect of the same forms differently disposed, some in position, some in growth and diminution, some in number, and some in color and other qualities.

For some have crests or combs on the head, or a mane, or bristles on the neck, while others do not. Some have bones, claws, and feathers, in place of which others have spines, hard soles, or scales. Some have teats on the chest, others on the belly, others near the haunches. Some have small limbs, others long ones; some few feathers, others many; some white, some black, some of mixed color.

They also differ according to their ways and manner of life, their nourishment, and the parts we have touched on briefly here; but further on we shall discuss this more fully and distinguish their kinds, parts, and characteristics.

Hence we say that some animals are aquatic, others live on land. Of the aquatic ones, some are free-swimming, others cling to rocks; of the free-swimming ones, some are fixed in one form and remain in the water, unable to live outside it, while others are not fixed in one form but change into another and can live outside the water, as does the scorpion-fish. Of those fixed in one form, some take in water, others air - as do certain birds, the dolphin, and the whale - and some take in neither air nor water within, since they have neither lungs nor gills, and yet live in the water and cannot live outside it. Of the fixed ones, some are so firmly attached that when they are detached from the rock they die, while others detach themselves, go off in search of food, and then return and reattach themselves to the rocks.
Of the land animals, some have lungs and breathe, others do not, such as bees, wasps, and segmented creatures.

There is another difference among animals with respect to motion: some only swim, others both swim and walk, like the crab family; some only walk, like the walking animals; some both walk and crawl, like the various kinds of lizards and certain worms; some only crawl, like serpents and earthworms.

Among birds, some only fly, and of these some have weak feet, like the swallow and the like, while some lack feet entirely, like the [reading uncertain: damrim], some only walk, since they have few feathers, and some both fly and walk.

The difference among animals with respect to their manner of life is this: some, it is said, are social, some solitary, and some display both dispositions. Of the social ones, some have a proper place or dwelling, others do not; of those that have a dwelling, some store up food in common, others do not; and of those that store food in common, some eat and preserve a reserve, others eat without preserving one.
Solitary animals are those that have hooked claws, and those that associate poorly with others.
Man, however, is sometimes found alone, sometimes among a crowd.
Of the animals mentioned above, some eat flesh and other animals, some grain, some grasses, some roots, and some a food peculiar to themselves, as bees do.
And some seek their food by day, others by night.

They also differ in gentleness and anger, boldness and timidity, dullness and cleverness, silence and noisiness, wantonness and chastity; and generally, every animal that makes sound with its mouth, man excepted, is especially noisy and clamorous at the time of mating.

All animals share three organs in common: the mouth, the belly, and the organ of excretion; and whatever has a bladder also has a belly, though not conversely. In some the sex is distinguishable, in others not; and where sex is distinguishable, the male is the agent and the female the one acted upon, and those that generate offspring like themselves have organs of conception and birth - the female possessing a womb, or something answering to a womb. Some generate live young, as man does, and all hairy animals, and the great sea creatures such as the dolphin and the whale; others generate eggs, and others worms, as will be told below. In all of them the sense of touch resides in a homogeneous organ, such as flesh or the like; but the operative and locomotive powers reside in the heterogeneous organs. In all animals there is blood, or something answering to blood, and an organ that receives it; and no blood is found in animals that have more than four principal parts.

All animals share in common either motion of the whole body or motion of parts: the primary animals move by feet, wings, head, tail, ribs, or various undulations. Some have two feet, some four, some are many-footed, and in all animals the feet come in pairs. Among fish, some move by fins - that is, by wing-like organs whose ends are drawn together - some by the head, as the Greeks call the soft-fleshed creatures; some by feet and tail, like the lobster; and some by their whole bulk, as the Greeks call the cetaceans. Among flying creatures, some have two wings, some four; and of these, some have leathery wings, some do not; and of those with leathery wings, some have what resembles feathers, and blood, and two feet, like the bat, others do not. Wrinkled creatures have no blood at all, whatever their kind; and of these, those with four wings sting with a stinger, like bees, while those with two wings sting with something like a little proboscis, like flies.

Thus far extends this proper part, which is divided into two: the first, extending from the beginning up to the passage 'and all animals share three organs in common,' dealt with the differences among animals in general; the second, following on from it, treats of their points of agreement.
On the external and internal limbs of man

It is fitting that we speak first of the limbs of man, the noblest and most worthy of all animals, and the best known to us, and necessarily the most distinct from the rest - his relation to the other animals being like that of gold and silver to the other metals. And although the limbs of man are known to the senses, we discuss them in order to give their causes, first the instrumental or organic limbs, afterward the homogeneous ones.

The head is divided into the skull and the face. On the skull the hair grows, and the skull is divided into the crown, the vertex, and the occiput, and the crown contains the brain. The occiput, however, is hollow, and the skull of a woman has a single suture running around it, while the skull of men has many sutures; and on the face, the part above, which lies below the suture, is called the forehead. A large forehead signifies a lazy person of poor judgment, a small one signifies an agile and good person; a broad forehead signifies indiscretion, a round one, irascibility. Below the forehead are the eyebrows, and those that follow a straight line signify a womanish softness; arched eyebrows extending to the point of the nose signify a sharp and studious person, while those that slope down to the prominences of the cheeks signify a negligent person of perverse disposition. Drooping eyebrows signify an envious person.

The eyelids lie beneath the eyebrows, and where they meet they form two corners, and two tear-ducts. When the tear-duct, and what follows the corner of the eye, is small and delicate, it denotes malice of disposition and habit; if fleshy, it signifies base cunning; a moderate condition is praiseworthy. Eyelids that close rarely denote a foolish and shameless person; when they close very often and frequently, they express a noble but indiscreet nature; a moderate blinking indicates a discreet and well-disposed person.

Within the eyelids are the eyes. In the eyes there is moisture, and in the middle is the pupil, in which is its opening, surrounded by the white; and the pupil-opening of the eyes varies in man and in the horse, being large in some, not in others. It may be dark, inclining to redness, which is then a sign of sharpness and discernment; or it may be grey in others, and sometimes there is a marked greyness. Prominent eyes with much movement signify a disturbance of judgment, while deep-set eyes demonstrate sharpness in all animals; those of moderate size, neither too prominent nor too deep-set, are praiseworthy - and almost all animals have eyes, or something answering to them.

The ears are on the head, and their composition is of cartilage and flesh; the ears have two parts, an inner one and an outer, cavernous one; and in the inner part is a winding passage terminating in a corresponding bone, to which passage hearing and ringing sounds reach, and from which they return to the brain; and veins go out from the brain and come to the ears, and the movement of the ears takes place over them. Among hearing animals in general, man included, some have full ears, others only the openings for ears, as with birds and scaly creatures; and prominent ears in men are a sign of stupidity and garrulousness - moderate ones are praiseworthy - and very hairy ears in a man are not a sign of good hearing. Between the ears and the eyes is the prominence of the cheeks.

The nose is the organ of smell, and the wall in the middle of the nostrils is made of cartilage, and properly speaking breathing occurs through the nostrils. Breathing through the mouth is foul and contrary to nature, done only from necessity; and sneezing, from wind multiplied in the brain, is expelled through the nose, and is taken by men to be a sign of something to come at that time - though truly it is a sign of good sense and vigor.
The lips lie below the nostrils, made of flesh capable of good movement; within them are the gums, made of flesh, in which are the teeth, within which are the tongue and palate.
The tongue is of soft flesh, and is the organ of taste at its outermost tip, while lower down, in its broader part, lies a different sensation.

It also has the sense of touch throughout its whole extent, and when knotted it produces a lisping or muteness, while a tongue of a shape between broad and narrow is well suited to movement and fitting speech.
In the palate there is a structure fitted to the voice, above the windpipe; and it is a dangerous organ if it swells.
The neck lies between the head and the chest. In front of it is a single windpipe made of cartilage, which is the organ of voice and breathing.
And there is another passage behind it, called the esophagus, or mouth of the stomach, made of flesh attached to the vertebrae of the neck.

The chest, open in front, has two parts in which are the breasts, made of soft, spongy flesh, the organs of milk in the female; in the male they sometimes have milk too. Below the chest is the belly, and in the belly is the navel, the root of the belly, and below the belly is the pubic region, around which are the groins, and around the groins are the two hips; and at the end of the pubic region is the penis, made of flesh, cartilage, and sinews, whose tip is the foreskin, whose head is called the glans; and below the penis are the glandular testicles. In the female, in place of the penis, is the womb; and the penis and the womb are the passage for urine and for seed.

What lies behind the hips is the region of the angle, beneath which is the head of the hip bone, and from there come the thighs and the knees, and above the knees is the kneecap, then the shins, of which the front part is called the shin proper, and the back the calf; then come the ankles, and behind the foot is the heel, and below the foot is the sole, while above it, made of many bones and sinews, is called the instep of the foot; then come the toes, and at the tips of the toes are the nails.
If the sole of the foot is so fleshy that one walks upon the flesh itself, this signifies a dull and ill-disposed person.

As for the arms: the first bone is called the upper-arm bone, and it is single; in the other part there are two bones; and if this bone is diminished, so too are the hip and, likewise, the hand and foot; and at the end of the arm is the hand, whose inner surface is the palm, and whose outer or upper surface is the back of the hand, which is divided into five fingers, and in each finger there are three joints and three bones, except in the thumb, which has two; and when two or three lines are found dividing the whole palm, this signifies length of life.
What lies behind the belly is the back, and on the back are the shoulder blades and the vertebrae. On the sides, which connect the back to the chest, are the ribs, eight on either side.

These limbs are commonly found in both male and female, and are known by the senses. We have spoken of them so as to complete the plan of the book's overall design, and so as to compare them with the limbs of other animals, and to give their causes, leaving nothing hidden. And we say that man is composed according to the arrangement of the universe, for he has an above and a below, a right and a left, a front and a back.
The other animals, however, hold their heads down toward the earth, and either do not have all the same limbs as man, or if they do, these are not arranged in the same way.
After this let us speak of the internal organs of man, and of the animals that approach his nature.

We say, then, that the brain of man is large in proportion to his size, and is placed at the front of the head, and is divided into two; and behind it is another brain, in the ventricle of the head, separated from the front part; and there is no blood at all in the brain, nor any vein, and it has a membrane resembling thin leather, in which are veins, and above this membrane is a thin, fragile bone at the crown.

In the neck, in creatures that have lungs, is the windpipe, surrounded by fine veins, positioned directly opposite the nasal passage; it has an opening leading to the mouth, and has an epiglottis between those two openings, which covers the passage to the lung so that nothing from food falls into it; and that passage branches into two toward the wings of the lung, as appears in birds and quadrupeds, in which the branching of the lung is visible; and through this passage the lung takes in air, and it is connected to the great vein and also to the heart, and is the pathway of breath.
The esophagus is placed alongside the windpipe, attached to it, and is the mouth of the stomach on the side of the mouth, and its structure is of flesh capable of stretching and expanding.

The belly of man is divided into an upper and a lower part; the upper resembles the belly of a dog, from which comes the rectum, broad and only slightly twisted; the lower belly resembles that of a pig, and leads to the outlet of the dry residue.
Above the intestine is something resembling a membrane, attached to the thick vein and to the aorta, in which are many veins, thick from top to bottom.

The heart has three chambers, and is placed where the windpipe of the lung branches; the pointed part of the heart is set toward the front, above the chest, and its substance is of thick, hard flesh; in man it inclines somewhat to the left side, and the left chamber is large, the middle one moderate, the right one small; and the middle and right chambers are perforated, their openings facing toward the lung; and the large chamber is connected to the great vein and to the middle vessel, while the middle chamber is connected to the aorta; and the veins in the heart branch out to the vessels of the lung, so that through them breath is restored to the heart.

The lung is of soft, spongy flesh, greatly inflatable, and has passages coming from the great vein; it has more blood than any other part of the animal's body, and blood flows out of it quickly, not being fixed there - whereas in the heart the blood is fixed.
Below the lung is the wall of the chest, bordering the sides, the ribs, and the top of the neck.

Below this wall is the liver, on the right side; in man it is round, and in it is the vessel of red bile, connected to the great vein; and the spleen is on the left, connected only to the great vein, and the human spleen is long and narrow, resembling the spleen of a pig.

Then come the kidneys, placed upon the vertebrae; from the great vein and the aorta come two veins that enter the depths of each kidney, resembling little cavities, and no blood is found in these kidney cavities; and from the depth of each kidney come two strong, hard veins; and from the middle of each kidney comes a sinewy vessel that reaches the vertebrae of the back and the hips and the bladder, which is the last of the internal organs; and the bladder hangs from the passages leading from the kidneys to the root of the penis and to the testicles, of which we shall speak below. We have summarized these matters in general, since we are speaking to the learned.
Here ends the first book.

In the second book he treats of the limbs of brute animals: first the external ones, then the internal, in the same general manner. And in the first part, first of the limbs of quadrupeds, second of the limbs of flying creatures, third of the limbs of fish; and he said that in different kinds of animals the limbs generally vary in shape.

Quadrupeds that bear live young have a head, and on the head some have horns, some do not; and those that do, for the most part, have a cloven hoof, like the ram, the stag, and those with a single horn; some cloven-hoofed animals, like the arkas, some not, like the Indian donkey. The horns of animals are hollow except those of the stag, and no animal sheds its horns except the stag, save by accident; and some horns are twisted, some not; some curve backward, some forward.
Animals have hairs on the upper eyelid. The eyes will be discussed further below, as will the nose.

The neck of animals is made of separate rings, except that of the lion, in which the neck-bone is continuous. In quadrupeds the front feet take the place of hands, and are smaller than or equal to the hind feet, except in the elephant, where they are much larger. The elephant uses as a hand a kind of tube, which is its trunk in place of a hand; through it, it takes food and drink and brings them to its mouth, and through it, it breathes. Animals that bear live young bend their front legs forward and their hind legs backward; man does the opposite. Egg-laying quadrupeds, like lizards, bend forward, and there is no animal that bends both its front and back legs backward. The joints near the shoulder bend in the opposite direction to the joints near the buttocks. Some animals have fixed feet, some do not.

Some animals have teats on the chest, like man; some on the belly, like the sow and the dog; some near the haunches, like cows, sheep, and goats. Some have four teats, two nipples on each side, like cows, some do not. Man, however, is the opposite.
Quadrupeds, for the most part, have a tail; some are hairy all over, some have a mane, like the lion, some have a crest of hair, and some are hairy in front and only partly so behind.

As for flying creatures, know that a bird has a head and a neck, a back and a front, an upper and a lower part; and they have feet, which they bend backward. Birds of prey have large haunches and a strong chest, and every bird has fixed feet, and some have webbing joining their toes; a bird has four toes, three in front and one behind in place of a heel. Some kinds have two toes in front and two behind, like the owl. Birds have a beak, and the passage of the nose is in the beak, and the passage of hearing is in the head; they have a mouth and eyes, and they have feathers and tails, and some birds have crests, some combs, like the hoopoe and the lark.

As for fish, it is known that some have a head, a front, and a back part, and no kind of fish has a neck, and they have no penis, testicles, or teats, except the dolphin and the whale. They have no visible organs of mating, and they have gills through which they draw in water and expel it; some have two fins, some four; some have scales, some skin, and they have blood; and a certain fish is able to hold ships fast by a natural property.
The serpent kind falls between land animals and water animals, for some remain in water, some on land, and those in the water stay close to the banks; of these we shall speak further below.
On the internal organs

After this let us speak of the internal organs of animals, and we say that animals have water in their eyes, and if the eyes of serpents and swallows are pierced and that water is drawn out, they will be healed and their sight will return.
Some animals have teeth, some have horny ridges instead, and of those with teeth, some have them in the upper jaw, some do not.
And those with horns have neither such ridges nor upper teeth.
Man sheds his teeth, as do certain other animals, and the teeth of young dogs are sharp and white, while those of old dogs are the opposite.
The teeth of an old horse are white.
Animals with many teeth are, for the most part, long-lived.
All fish have sharp teeth, and some have a thin, rough tongue, with teeth upon it and upon the gums.
The teeth of serpents are sharp and set close together like a saw.
Animals have an upper and a lower jaw, and all that have them move the lower one, except the crocodile; and they have a tongue.

The dog's tongue has healing power, and the elephant's tongue is very small; some animals have long tongues, some broad ones, and the tongues of serpents are thin, long, black, forked in two, and protrude a great deal.

Animals have one passage to the lung and another to the stomach, and certain kinds of fish do not have this second passage, for their stomach is attached directly to the head, and they sometimes eject their stomach outward.

Animals that have horns and lack upper teeth have four stomachs: the first is large and rough within; the second is smaller than it; the third is equal to it in size; and after the third comes the fourth, which is shaggy, and after that the intestine.
Those that have teeth in both jaws have a single stomach, such as man, the lion, the dog, the horse, the bear, and the wolf, and after the stomach comes the intestine.
The intestines of serpents are similar to those of egg-laying quadrupeds, and the belly of the serpent is narrow; the intestines of birds and of fish are slender. They have ribs around the belly.
Serpents have thirty ribs, matching the number of days in a month.

Some birds have a crop, such as the hen, the dove, and the partridge; the crop is made of a skin-like membrane, and in it undigested food is held; it is attached to the liver, and the liver is hard, covered by a strong membrane.
Some birds do not have a crop, but do have a stomach.
The passage leads to the lung, and all creatures that breathe have a lung; some do not breathe, such as fish and segmented creatures, and therefore lack one.

Animals have a heart, and in all animals the heart is placed in the middle of the chest, except in man; and the pointed part of the heart in animals inclines toward the interior of the chest, while in fish the pointed part hangs toward the head, and passages go out from the heart toward each of the gills in fish; and the hearts of animals contain no bone, except the heart of the cow, the stag, and the horse.

Animals have a liver, and some animals have bile in the liver, some have none at all, such as the dolphin, and some have it in the intestines, such as doves; some have bile in both liver and intestine, such as the hawk and the kite; some have it in the liver, intestine, and stomach; some in the ears; and some in the skin of the liver.
The spleen is present in some, absent in others; it is on the left side, though sometimes the liver is on the left and the spleen on the right, in which case it is very small.
Live-bearing quadrupeds have kidneys and a bladder, but egg-laying quadrupeds, birds, and fish have neither kidneys nor bladder.
On the penis, testicles, and womb

Thus far we have spoken of the organs serving the life of the individual; it remains now to speak of the organs serving generation, and first let us speak of the penis and testicles, then of the womb.

We say that in some the penis is made of cartilage and flesh, as in man; in others of sinew, as in the camel and stag; in others of bone, as in the wolf and fox; and some are freely prominent, while others are bound to the belly.
The penis is the outlet of urine and of seed, and through it some animals urinate backward, such as the camel and the lion, and some forward. Females, for the most part, urinate backward.

Some lack testicles, such as fish, and some have them; and of those that have them, some have them internally, attached to the vertebrae, some near the belly; and some have them externally, some hanging free, as in man, some near the belly, as in the dolphin and the footless creatures. Serpents have two passages running from the region of the flank to the region of the vertebrae.

These converge at the outlet of the residue, and two vessels come from the aorta without blood, and each reaches to the tip of each testicle; and two other veins, full of blood, come from the kidneys and reach the testicles; and from the region of the testicles two channels converge at the front of the penis, and another channel comes from the bladder to the penis.

Wombs differ between animals that bear live young and those that lay eggs. The extremities of the womb divide into two, to the left and to the right, and the opening of the womb is made of flesh and sinew; the diversity of wombs is apparent in dissection. For this reason we pass over it briefly, so as to come to the giving of causes for these matters. Thus far we have spoken of the heterogeneous organs.
Here ends the second book.

Now we must speak of the homogeneous organs, first of the solid ones, such as veins, sinews, skins and membranes, bones and ribs and the like, then of the soft and liquid ones, such as flesh, blood, marrow, and the like. And in the first part he treats first of the organs that carry blood and sensation - namely the veins and sinews - and second of the supporting organs, such as the bones and their kind.

And he said: 'Since blood and the veins are the origins from which the heart is formed, we shall speak of their arrangement' - and we ourselves feel a certain dread in undertaking to describe the branching of the veins, the sinews, and all the organs of animals, knowing that in each and every one of these there is a single root. And after they branch, if they were to be rejoined, that would be a marvel indeed. For we see that in trees, once the branches have divided - branches which likewise have, each in its own way, pith, membrane, hard tissue, veins, sap, and their sinew-like fibers, and so on - there is never a rejoining of these; and even if they are forcibly pressed together, branch is never joined to branch such that the veins of one are not still separate from the veins of the other, unless a knot is formed through which what is supplied on one side is passed on to the other. And likewise the veins there are distinct, each supplying what it can and however it may; so how could anyone's heart rise so high as to dare to describe the branching of the veins and sinews and the other organs, when, the further they withdraw from their first principle - which is the heart - the more, perhaps, they are never truly rejoined, but are divided into separate parts; or perhaps, if they are joined, they are bound by so fine and imperceptible a junction that it strikes our minds with dread. And for this reason certain physicians have erred, especially because they made their observations by the senses alone - some of them on a dead animal, in which the veins and sinews suddenly contract as the blood leaves; others on a living animal, in which they attempted to examine the nature of the veins and sinews, whose principles and origins lie hidden within. By what path, then, can we proceed, except a slippery one, groping in the dark at what may in fact be otherwise? Let the one who understands, understand this, and let him be
humble of heart.

I say, then, on this matter, following with due caution the foremost of the philosophers, as coming closest to the truth, that the heart has three chambers, as we touched on above. The right one is the largest, full of blood; the left is the smallest; and the middle one lies between them. The two smaller chambers are perforated as far as the lung. One great vein proceeds from the largest chamber, from its upper right side, and another vein - namely the aorta - proceeds from the middle chamber, on the left side.

The great vein lies toward the front, the aorta toward the back. The great vein is formed of membrane and skin-like tissue, the aorta of skin-like tissue alone. The great vein divides into two parts, one going to the region above the heart, the other to the region below it; and the branch going above the heart divides into two, one of which goes to the lung, dividing again into two according to the lung's own division - and these branch further into many within the lung, suffusing it with blood. The other branch goes to the vertebrae and to the last ring of the neck; the one going to the vertebrae sends branches to each of the ribs and to each vertebra; the one going to the last ring of the neck branches to the hollows of both shoulders, to the two bones of the forearm and the fingers on each side, and, on the other side, up through the neck to the membrane of the brain and to the organs of sense.

The part of this great vein that goes below the heart branches and passes to the liver and the spleen; the branch going to the liver divides into two, one going to the flank, the other to the armpit and the right forearm bone, and it is this branch that is diminished in cases of liver pain; and from the branch going to the spleen, another goes to the left forearm bone and branches on the left side.
And from this vein below the heart a branch proceeds to the stomach, the intestine, the caul, and the mouth of the stomach.

The aorta divides into two strong vessels, one to the bladder, the other to the kidneys; and from the kidneys to the hips and to the male member in males and the womb in females. No vessel goes from the great vein to the womb, but many come from the aorta; and from both the great vein and the aorta come many large, blood-empty vessels to the region of the testicles, and to the hips, legs, feet, and toes.

And I say that the veins have a single point of origin, from which they arise, namely the heart - not the head, as Sartinoz said, nor the belly, as Dianoz held, nor four major regions, as Diogenes claimed.

But the heart is the origin both of the veins and of the sinews; yet the formation of the sinews is not a single continuous structure from one root, as is the formation of the veins. The sinews are distributed at the joints and bends of the bones, and in the parts suited to the body's strength, such as the shoulders of the back, the arms, the legs, and the hollows of the knees; and they are most numerous in the feet and hands, the ribs, the neck, and the ligaments of the shoulder blades. A sinew is generated and nourished from the viscous moisture that surrounds it. Sinews, once severed, do not rejoin; veins, however, do. In the head there are no sinews, but only the serial sutures. Certain fibers are found woven between the nature of sinew and vein, occurring between sinews and veins, and they serve motion; a watery fluid is found in them resembling the watery part of blood. Similar fibers are found in the blood of certain animals, such that when they are drawn out the blood does not clot; these are not found in the blood of the stag, the hare, and similar animals by nature, and for this reason their blood clots only weakly, like milk without rennet.

The skin is continuous throughout, on account of the pores, the nails, and the five openings of the senses. Skin in a place without flesh beneath it, if cut, does not heal back together, as in the thinness of the cheeks, the tip of the foreskin, and the eyelid. Human skin, relative to its extent, is very thin among skins, and has a viscous mucilage, from which glue is made. Skin that has been cut feels nothing.

Bones and organs have membranes. There are two membranes of the head: the first is called the dura mater, and is stronger and harder; the other is called the pia mater, and encloses the brain. The membrane of the heart is large, and the caul that lies about the kidneys of rams has a membrane, and the bladder resembles a membrane. Egg-laying creatures have no membrane, except lizards, and this from a dry surplus. A stone can form in the bladder. Moisture does not leave the bladder of the dead.

The bones are arranged one to another and fitted together, as can be seen starting from the head. The skull is, in some creatures, a single piece without sutures; in others there are sutures, as in man, in whom there are six sutures, two near the ears and four in the remaining region. The skull-sutures of women are rounded; in men they meet at the lowest point, and the jaw is joined to the skull, as appears in man, in whom the head is joined to the vertebrae of the neck and back, and to the hard hip-bones and the feet; and above, the bones of the shoulder-sockets are attached to the vertebrae and the back and the ribs, and the bones forming the shoulder blades are attached on one side to the shoulder blades and on the other to the bones of the forearm, the upper arm, and the wrist.

In the bones of some animals there is marrow, in others none; in some it is scanty, and present in only a few bones, as in the lion, which has marrow only in the bones of the forearm and thighs, and even there it is scanty and thin. The lion's bones are so hard that fire can be struck from them by friction; and some animals, in place of bones, have spines and cartilage.

Perhaps bone, spine, and cartilage share a common nature, differing in hardness and softness; and none of them heals back together once cut off, nor do they grow again. And in the bodies of animals there are organs that resemble neither bone nor cartilage, namely the horns. Thus far we have spoken of the organs generated from seed.

From the surplus of food, however, are generated horns, hard soles, and hooves; and claws, and the beaks of birds, and these can bend, whereas bones cannot. They do not grow far beyond their original formation, and their colors follow the color of the skin and hair. Some horns are hollow, some not. No animal sheds its horns except the stag, which sheds them every year, unless it is castrated.

Hair occurs in animals that bear live young, and it varies in length and shortness, in coarseness and fineness, according to the organs and the skin: for on coarse skin the hair is coarse, and on parts of much moisture the hair is soft, like wool - and conversely, conversely.

In hot regions the hair is stiff, in cold regions soft; straight hair is soft, curly hair stiff; and sometimes hair hardens so much that it comes to resemble spines, and claws so much that they resemble bone; and in general, hair and nails grow harder after death, and an animal of varied color in its hair is likewise varied in its skin.

The color of the hair follows the color of the skin, except in man; and in some creatures the color of the hair changes with a change of water, for the hair of animals that drink from a certain river turns black, from another white, and from another red.

And if mating occurs after drinking a certain water, the lamb will be black; and especially in old age, man's hair turns grey, as does the horse's, and sometimes the hair whitens from the root, sometimes from the very tip.

And the first kind is properly called greyness. Dryness is not the cause of greying, for it is impossible for something to be dry from the root of its own growth. Hair turns grey both from illness and from nature.

Greyness arising from illness can be cured, and hair turns grey when covered over, and from the retaining of breath through blockage of the nostrils. Greying begins at the front and at the temples, and the hair of the head, eyebrows, and eyelashes is born with a person; afterward, hair grows first on the pubic region, second in the armpits, third on the beard.

Hair falls out first from the head, at the front; but the back of the head never goes bald; and in a person castrated before the age of producing seed, hair does not grow there at all; and if castration occurs afterward, the hair falls out, except that of the pubic region. Some go bald from frequent intercourse, while others experience the opposite, since hair grows there because of it; and if hair falls out in youth, it grows back - but afterward it grows back sparsely and poorly bearded, and such a person will scarcely go bald. And if the menses are retained, women grow beards. Men and women with few hairs, which appear only later, rarely have seed or offspring, especially if they lack pubic hair. The hair of the beard and head grows abundantly, and likewise the eyebrows of some, on account of the moisture that escapes when the bones on which it grows separate; and in old quadrupeds hair multiplies. The hair and scales of fish thicken and harden after mating, and the colors of the feathers of certain birds change according to the seasons, and according to the qualities of the seasons, and according to age; and a feather that has been cut does not grow back from the root - hair, however, does.
On the soft and liquid parts

Flesh, and what resembles it, lies between the bones and the skin. It is found in blooded animals, and when cut lengthwise or crosswise, it grows back. Flesh is scanty when the internal organs are large, and when they are small, the flesh is fatty.

The caul is suet, and differs from fat, because the caul congeals and breaks or crumbles when rubbed between the fingers, whereas fat melts. Fat lies between the skin and the flesh; the caul, however, lies within the flesh, and creatures with teeth in both jaws have fat, while those lacking upper teeth have caul instead. Properly speaking the caul is like a net, and hangs from the greater stomach; and caul is also generated around the heart, the kidneys, the liver, and the spleen. Sheep die if their kidneys become covered over with caul, and for this reason they should be moved from overly rich pastures. The caul of fish is mixed with fat, and for this reason does not congeal.

Blood is necessary and natural in those that have it. It is in the veins, and in no other organ except the heart. It has no sensation of touch; in taste it is naturally sweet; it is red, and hot and moist while it remains in the heart. Outside the body it congeals, except in the stag, the hare, and creatures of similar nature - unless certain fibers are drawn out of it. The blood of the bull congeals faster than any other. Coarse-blooded animals have little blood. Blooded creatures putrefy quickly. Blood pulses in the veins, and in animals that bear live young it is thick and dark, especially in the bull and the donkey; and in the lower part of the body it is thicker and darker than in the upper, and it is not found to be extremely thick or extremely thin except by chance.

In the embryo blood first appears in the heart, and when it becomes abundant it thins and grows watery, and for this reason a man may sometimes sweat blood. When it is abundant it induces sickness, and when scanty it induces death. When an animal sleeps, the blood gathers inward. Well-cooked and digested blood turns into suet, and from putrid blood comes venom, and from that, pus.

A woman's blood is thicker and darker than a man's, and woman has more blood in abundance than the females of other animals, and for this reason she menstruates. In the young it is abundant, thin, and watery; in the old, thick, dark, and scanty. And an old person's blood congeals faster, both inside and outside the body, than a young person's.

Marrow is bloody in the young, but fatty in the old. Marrow is found in the hollow bones, and in some it is entirely absent, even though the bones are hollow, and in some it is scanty, as in the bones of the pig. All the body's fluids are contained in their own proper vessels, as blood in the veins, marrow in the bones, and so with the rest. These fluids are generated along with the bodies of the animals themselves; milk and seed, however, are generated afterward.

Milk is in the teats, and in milk there is a watery part - that is, whey - and a coarse part, which is cheese, and an oily part, which we call butter. The thicker it is, the more cheese it contains, and the more nourishing it is. Also because of heat, the milk of dark-skinned women is more nourishing than that of fair-skinned women. The milk of the donkey is thin, and the mare's even thinner; the camel's milk is the thinnest of all; and beans and vetch increase milk. However, vetch does not suit pregnant ewes, since it burdens the birth. And before pregnancy, an animal naturally has no milk.

Nevertheless, animals sometimes have milk from the plants they eat; and in a certain land, goats' udders are rubbed with nettles, and first blood comes out, then pus, and afterward good milk, even though they are not pregnant.
In the teats of males there is no milk, except very rarely.
And there was a he-goat that had milk from which cheese was made, and he had a son that likewise had milk.
The milk of animals lacking teeth in the upper jaw curdles; other milk does not.
It is curdled with rennet, or with fig-milk, with which the wool must first be soaked and then washed off with milk.
By that washing other milk is curdled; and rennet is not found in animals with teeth in both jaws, except in the hare.
Rennet is effective against flux, especially that of the hare.
Six times as much cheese is made from cow's milk as from goat's milk.
Seed is white and thick, and congeals with heat, but with cold it liquefies and turns dark.
Hairy animals have viscous seed, and when placed in water, if it sinks to the bottom, it is fit for generation.
Here ends the third book.
Thus far we have treated of blooded animals. Now we must take up bloodless animals, of which there are three kinds.

The first kind is soft-shelled, called in Greek malachia, and has two species: one is soft both within and without, like the octopus; the other has flesh outside and something like a spine within, in the manner of the cuttlefish.

The second kind is hard-shelled, and this too has two varieties: one has soft flesh within and a hard shell without that does not break or crack when bent, such as the crab family and the tortoise; the other is of the same kind, but its shell breaks when bent, such as the oyster and the snail.

The third kind is segmented, and creatures of this sort are hard both within and without; in their bodies there is neither bone nor flesh, but something whose nature lies between flesh and bone, and this segmentation occurs either in the belly, or in the back, or over the whole body, as in the many-footed creature that is segmented over its whole body. Of this kind, some have wings, like bees and wasps, some do not; and of those without wings, some never have them, like certain kinds of ants, while some do not have them at first but grow them later, like certain other kinds of ants, and glow-worms.
And so these three kinds multiply into seven or nine kinds.

We pass briefly over matters of this sort for two reasons: first, because for the most part he treats of creatures that are not found among us, or if they are found among us, their names are unknown to us; second, because for the most part he will repeat all this in the second part, when he comes to set out the reasons for the causes of the organs.

And he said: the malachia, as regards its external organs, has a head and feet, and what lies between these - between the belly and the feet - and it has eight feet, though one species of it has many feet.

The cuttlefish, the octopus, and certain others have two long appendages, hard at the tip, by which they take food and bring it to the mouth; and they move these like oars, and also use the feet that are near the eyes in place of hands and arms.

The root of the other feet is toward what takes the place of the spine, and their tips are divided in two, and it grasps and holds things with these attachments - but when it is on sand it cannot hold anything with them.
In the part above the feet there is a channel through which it expels the water that reaches its interior from the sea, and this water is discharged to the left, and sometimes to the right.
Through that organ the males discharge their seed, and it swims upon its head.
Its head is hard and swollen while it lives. It expands itself in a strange way, since its eyes are on top of its head, and its mouth is behind, and it looks toward its feet.

Among the many-footed creatures and the other kinds of malachia with eight feet, there is a difference: the many-footed ones have small bodies and long feet, while the others have large bodies and short feet; and all species of malachia have a skin that covers their bodies.

In the internal parts of the malachia, after the mouth comes the esophagus, then a crop as in birds, then a coiled stomach, then the intestine, and the organ containing the seed and eggs, which lies beneath the mouth.
When it is afraid, it discharges what is contained in this organ, and thereby clouds the water through this,

so as to hide itself and escape. The many-footed creatures of the malachia kind have nothing hard within their bodies, but around the head they have a cartilage that stiffens and hardens when touched, and in what serves as their nostrils are gill-like openings. There is a single passage from the brain to the lower part of the body, but in females there are two, and below these passages are red bodies containing the eggs and seed. The cuttlefish has white eggs resembling hail; and among the kinds of malachia, especially in the cuttlefish, the bodies of the males are rougher than those of the females, and darker in front than behind. The many-footed creatures of this kind are of many species, for there is one that lives in water and one that lives on land, and these are of different species.

The mode of the hard-shelled animals is, as said above, of two kinds: some have a shell that breaks, and among these are found both a land kind, such as the snail and the tortoise, and a sea kind, such as the oyster and the crab; and in both there are those with feet and those without. Among the sea kind we clearly see that some are attached to rocks and die if separated, while others are attached but sometimes detach and sometimes reattach; and of those that attach, some have movement in their whole body, some only in parts, since, although they do not move from place to place, they nonetheless contract and extend. And it appears that some of these have only the sense of touch. They have a place from which they take in food, and a place where they deposit waste, though in some of them this is found in the belly - and in this they resemble plants.
Of those that do not attach themselves, some have five legs on each side, some six, some seven - four larger and three more slender.
Some swim with the tail, as is seen partly in lobsters and crab-kinds, and they have what resemble long horns, and other, shorter ones, at whose tips are eyes of hard skin.
They have a mouth and teeth, and some of them move the upper jaw, like the crayfish.

They have an intestine and an opening through which they expel waste and seed, and many of them have the mouth below and the place of excretion above, on the back, as in the sea-urchin and many other kinds.
And some of these have a single stomach, in a small membrane.
And some have a stomach divided into five parts, as does the sea-urchin, and the differences in the internal and external organs of these animals are innumerable.

Of these and of the others there are almost countless kinds, of many species and many varieties, and Aristotle gave the names of some of them, but for the most part both the creatures themselves and their names are unknown to Latins and Arabs alike.

The segmented creatures are of many species, such as wasps, bees, flies, and the like, and they have a head, a belly, a chest, and a back between these. In many of them there is a single such structure, as in the long-bodied, many-footed animals. And they all live for a while after being cut. If cut in the middle, both halves will move and walk about. Among their organs of sense, all of them clearly have eyes.

Some have something resembling a tongue, and a soft or hard organ through which they take in food. Some sting with this same organ, such as those lacking a stinger, like flies and gnats. Of those with a stinger, some have it on the outside, like the scorpion, some on the inside, like bees and wasps. The scorpion, and the creature resembling it, has two stingers.

Among the segmented creatures, some have two wings, namely those that lack a stinger at the rear, like flies. Those that have a stinger at the rear have four wings. Some have membranous wings, like wasps, some do not. Some mate from behind, and some as other animals do. They have no flesh inside, and hence neither bones nor a spine. They have a mouth and an outlet for waste.
Some of them have a stomach and a flat, coiled intestine, as does the locust. Thus far he has treated of the vital organs.
On the organs of sense
Now he treats of the organs of sense.

And he says: the organs of the senses are not present in animals in a single manner. In some, all are found; in others, not. Man, and the walking, live-bearing animal, have all the organs of sense, which are: touch, taste, sight, hearing, and smell - except the mole.

All animals share in the sense of touch; otherwise they would never be nourished, nor move, whether by motion of the whole body or of parts, so as to pursue what is beneficial and flee what is harmful; and they have the organ for this.

And almost all have taste. For they favor what suits them, and those with a mouth like and dislike tastes, and desire what is familiar in food; and by this means some are caught. And they have eyes, and see. The mole, however, has this only as an accident of nature, at the time of birth; and if the skin over the place of the eyes is split open, something resembling eyes is found within, and the blackness of the eyes and the pupil appear, and from the brain come two strong nerves that reach the roots of the eyes. But sight and hearing are not apparent to us except in some creatures.

Fish hear, which is evident because they flee from sound, from voices, and from the noise of oars and ships. For this reason fishermen keep silent and command silence, and they cast their nets around; then they strike the water with stones and oars and shout, so that the fleeing fish run into the nets.
And some, clinging to rocks, are stunned by the noise and clamor, detach from the rocks, and fall, and are caught this way. Some have visible organs of hearing, some do not, though they do hear.

Some smell. Of these, some do not have visible nostrils. Fish, too, can smell, for they flee foul things, such as the water bailed out from the bottom of a ship, and when they sense the blood of other fish; and when fishing vessels are old and dirty they flee from their stench, and for this reason fishermen wash them.

Some are caught by the smell of salt, when it is placed at the mouth of their burrow, for they come out; and some are drawn to the smell of burnt things, and hunters catch them by this means. The kinds of malachia, hard-shelled creatures, and segmented creatures all have every sense.

Some of them die from the smell of sulfur. Ants flee their nests if sulfur and crushed wild rue are thrown into them. Many creatures flee and abandon their dwellings if someone smokes them out with smoke from a stag's horn.
The hedgehog, among all animals that have both skin and shell and walk on feet, hears the least and the most feebly.
Voice and sound follow upon these organs of sense, and for this reason Aristotle treats of them immediately afterward.

And he said: sound, voice, and speech are three distinct things. Animals lacking a lung emit sound: some by the rushing of air through their gill-openings, which lie below the jaws like a spine, as with certain fish; some also make sound through air passing between the wings and body when, in flying, they contract or extend, as flies, bees, and locusts do; and some by cleaving the water, as do the rays.

Voice, however, is produced only by means of the epiglottis, which is the end of the windpipe, and it is by the epiglottis that vocal sounds are articulated. Neither the windpipe nor the epiglottis exists except in creatures that have a lung. Voice varies and divides into many kinds: serpents hiss, the elephant trumpets, the crow caws, the sheep bleats, the horse neighs, the dog barks, the frog croaks. Among animals, in some the male and female cry out in the same manner, in others differently; in some only the male cries out, not the female, as with the cock and the male quail. Animals call to one another at the time of mating with a recognizable voice, and some also for food, and some for battle. The voices of animals within each species are alike; yet in some, the young do not cry out as their parents do, but as they are taught or grow accustomed to hearing. From this it appears that the form of the voice, and speech, are not natural, but follow the teaching of those who teach them.

Speech is made up of vocal sounds, and man alone speaks and converses. To speak or converse is to distinguish vocal sounds by means of the tongue. And note that voice and speech vary according to regions and places, since accordingly some have a wider and drier windpipe, some the opposite; and some a longer one, some shorter. Those deaf by nature are also mute; they have voice, however, not speech.
Children are not yet firm in their speech, just as they are not firm in their limbs; some never become fully firm, others only once they have advanced in age.

As for sleep and waking, it is certain that every blooded, walking creature both sleeps and wakes. And whatever has eyelids closes them in sleep. Man dreams, and so do the horse, the bull, the goat, the dog, and every live-bearing quadruped. A sign of this is seen in the neighing of horses and the barking of dogs in their sleep.

Egg-laying animals sleep little, and so do watery and soft-shelled creatures. This is known because they can be caught while asleep, not by their eyelids, since they have none. Fish sleep at the bottom of the sea, some on rocks, some in sand, and do not sense the fisherman.
The ray sleeps heavily, and the dolphin sleeps and snores while sleeping, and segmented creatures sleep, as bees do. Not dreaming is a sign of death or of sickness.

From the beginning up to this point he has treated of animals by distinguishing their limbs; from this point on he treats of animals according to their operations. And he treats of their operations in this manner: first according to generation and the preservation of the species, second according to the practice of natural industry in the regimen of life. And in the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth books he proceeds thus: in the fifth and sixth he treats of the generation of brute animals, in the seventh and eighth of the generation of man.
And he said: 'Male and female exist in some animals, but not in others.'
And just as some trees bear fruit and some do not, so too male and female bear offspring in some creatures and not in others, as with certain segmented creatures.
Some animals arise from male and female; some are generated without mating.
Some arise spontaneously, like trees; and some generate an incomplete creature, as the louse generates nits, and flies and small bees generate worms.

The female among animals is weaker, and has fewer sinews than the male, and finer hair, and moister flesh, and more slender legs and feet, and a thinner and higher voice - except for a few, such as the cow, whose voice is coarser than the bull's.
Among walking, blooded animals, the male is larger in body and longer-lived than the female, except in those that live by predation.

Among egg-laying creatures, however, the female is larger, with few exceptions, and the males, in most cases, have organs for fighting, such as horns and spurs; and in some, the horns of the females are stronger than those of the males.

In animals possessing male and female, mating occurs, and this differs by kind: in some the male mounts, in some the female sits, as the hen does; in some it takes place raised up, as with cranes; in some the pair lie stretched out on the ground, as wolves do. And some join back to back, as land hedgehogs do. Cows and crows, because of the hardness of the penis, mate while fleeing; among ferrets, the female positions herself beneath the male and calls him to mating.

The camel joins with the female from behind, continuing throughout the day, since it is a melancholic animal. The camel's penis is very hard, and bow-strings are made from it. The female elephant lies down and the male mounts her.
The egg-laying quadruped mates as the live-bearing quadruped does. Serpents mate entwined and coiled together. Rays mate back to back.

In some animals the female mounts, and live-bearing animals engage more in mating than egg-laying ones. The manner of mating varies among animals: some mate belly to belly, some back to back, some tail to tail, as do those that urinate backward. In some the male is placed beneath the female, and even here the manner varies, for in some the female places her belly over the male's back, in others over his belly, as spiders do.
On the season of mating

Some mate in autumn and winter, some at the beginning of summer, some at the end of spring, and some at every season, such as man and certain animals that live near him because of warmth and abundance of food, such as the hen, the pig, and the dog. Man desires mating in winter, woman in summer.

Many kinds of birds mate at the end of spring and the beginning of summer, laying eggs and rearing chicks. Wild birds mate and lay eggs once a year, swallows and martins twice. Domestic birds, however, mate and lay frequently, such as hens and doves, which mate and lay throughout the year, once December, near the winter tropic, has passed.
Some fish mate in winter, some in summer, some in autumn, some in spring, and some at every season.
Segmented creatures mate in winter, if the wind is southerly and the weather favorable.
A certain age is also required in animals for mating, and offspring differ accordingly: when animals first begin to produce seed, the seed is scant, and the offspring from it are weak and small.
Man produces seed on completing two periods of seven years, and he can beget children up to seventy years of age, and a woman up to fifty.

The organs of mating alter in size, shape, and appearance. The breasts of females become raised, and hair grows in the pubic region. The voice deepens because of the heat; and the voice of males, in some, becomes sharper, in others deeper.

Above he treated of the generation of perfect animals through mating; here he treats of the generation of imperfect animals without mating, such as shellfish and other hard-shelled creatures, and sponges. And by nature every hard-shelled animal is generated spontaneously in mud, and this varies with the variety of mud, for mud is found sometimes in sand, sometimes among rocks, and accordingly are generated oysters, mussels, cockles, horn-shells, razor-shells, and the like in the sea, and snails and tortoises on land, and other things like these.

And some are also generated within the shells of others, and some of these prepare a substance like wax, resembling egg-yolk, and discharge something like honey and like mucilage, and small offspring are generated from this. And some prepare something coiled, resembling honey, and then discharge something resembling a cluster of grapes, and generate from this.

Some generate in the depths of the sea, some near the shore; some in sand, some in mud; some move from their place, some do not - and all these grow quickly. In some of these, a substance resembling seed is found, so abundant that if pressed it soils the hand. Some of these swim and turn face upward toward the sky and receive the dew with great pleasure, as if receiving seed, and gather it within themselves, and from this comes the pearl.

The sponge is of three kinds. The first is loose in its texture; the second is denser; the third is very dense and quite tough - and for this reason it is placed under a helmet like padding, so as not to feel the blows. Sponges grow on rocks near the shore, and feed on mud, and have the sense of touch, since when touched they contract. And if it is separated from its place, it is fed upon by small fish.

If a part is cut and torn away from these sponges and thrown into the water, another creature is formed from it, resembling the one from which it was separated. In this it resembles a plant, whose branch, once in the ground, takes root and grows. Cold wind hardens the sponge, as happens to trees, and it rots in warm places. Some sponges are pale-colored, some are not, but are black, and have four or five channels, and resemble a lung in their structure.

The lobster, the crab, and other hard-shelled creatures like these are generated from mud. Sometimes some of them lay eggs between the tail and the chest, and the eggs resemble a cluster of grapes, and the stem of that cluster is cartilaginous. The cuttlefish too, an imperfect creature, nests in mud among sticks and warms its eggs for twenty nights, while other kinds of malachia are generated through mating, and their eggs are white. The many-footed creature lays eggs, and after some time generates a creature from them.
These matters have been treated in this fifth book in a general way, which ends here.
In the sixth book, which begins at this point, he specifies and divides the matter into three parts: first on birds, second on fish, third on quadrupeds.
On the generation of birds
At the time of mating the testicles of birds swell, and they are larger in those that mate more, such as the hen, and they shrink and diminish through frequent mating.
The seed of birds is white, as in other animals.
After the hen has received it, first the white appears, then the red, and after it has grown it becomes yellow, and afterward thickens.
The yolk is separated from the white, and on being laid it congeals and hardens.
Of eggs, some come from mating, some do not.

Those not from mating are called wind-eggs, and occur when hens or doves rub themselves against the ground, and some receive warm wind, as in summer, and lay eggs; or if someone touches them with the hand, they lay eggs in the same way.
And these are called wind-eggs.
The eggs of the cock, however, are said to come from mating, and after the hen has mated she shakes herself with a ruffling of feathers.
Hens, unless they sit upon their eggs, become sickly, and the eggs spoil.
The hen and the dove breed at every season, except during the two tropic months.
And so doves lay ten times a year, and in a certain region a hen lays forty eggs before brooding, and those that brood are more fertile than those that do not.
The hens called the adlamendos are large and long-bodied, of varied color, and lay every day, and kill their own chicks.
Some domestic hens lay twice a day.
Hens that lay a great deal die quickly.
Most birds lay in spring.
Birds of prey lay few eggs. Some lay in nests that they make of sticks, or of straw and hair and wool.
Some in holes in rock; some in holes in trees. Some build a nest of mud, like swallows and martins; some in trees; some on houses.
Some eggs are hard-shelled, some soft, like the eggs of crows. Some are white, like those of hens, doves, and partridges. Some are yellow, like those of birds dwelling around marshes.

Some are reddish, some speckled. Some eggs are pointed, some broad; some long, some short. Those that are long and pointed produce males; those that are short and round instead of pointed produce females.
Some eggs have two colors within: yellow in the middle and white around it. Some are yellow throughout.
The hen sits on her eggs for eighteen days in summer; in winter for nineteen, on the ground and in dung.
There was a certain drinker who placed eggs under a warm cushion and continued drinking until the chicks were formed.
When the hen has sat for three days, signs of the chick appear; from the white forms the substance of the chick, and from the yolk comes its nourishment.
In the white there appears something like a drop of blood, and this is the heart. From that point on, veins emerge in which there is blood.
These go to each of two membranes, one containing the white, the other the yolk.

In the membrane containing the white, blood appears; and of the two veins, one, going to the membrane containing the heart, serves to draw in air, while the other, going to the yolk, resembles an umbilical cord and serves to draw in nourishment; and gradually the head and eyes take shape, and when ten days have passed the chick is complete.
Its head is larger than its whole body, and the eyes are swollen, larger than a bean. The internal organs are apparent in it, and veins can be seen stretching from the heart to the eyes.

From the eyes veins go to the membrane containing the yolk; other veins go to the membrane enclosing the whole membrane in which the chick lies, and to the membrane of the yolk, and to the moisture that lies between these membranes.

The membranes are arranged in this way: there is the shell-membrane, and beneath it the membrane containing the chick and a certain moist substance; and there is another membrane within this, which separates the chick from that moisture; and beneath this moisture is the yolk, in its own membrane; and the umbilical cord stretches from the heart to this yolk.
And if the egg is broken before ten days,

the chick is found with its head above its right leg, and its wings above its head; and before this time the chick is, as it were, sleeping, and does not cry out, and bubbles appear around its heart and eyes, as if it wished to breathe.
Some hens produce twins, when two yolks are found in one egg; and as often happens with twins, one is smaller, and often deformed.

Doves are of various kinds: some are large, called torcate; some small, called saxeole, whose feet are rough and red; turtledoves resemble these; and there are other domestic kinds with feathered feet, and these lay at every season if kept in warm places and well fed.

Doves generally hatch one male and one female, and the male emerges first, the female after; the male dove sits on the eggs by day, the female by night, and they sit for twenty days; the female is more diligent in raising the young than the male, and they lay ten times a year, sometimes eleven.
In Egypt, however, they lay twelve times, and lay two eggs each time; the male mates with the female after a year, and once he has finished rearing his young, they lay again after fifteen days.
Those resembling them, namely turtledoves, lay two eggs, sometimes three, and turtledoves lay twice a year, sometimes three times, when the second clutch fails.
Some say that the turtledove mates after three months, that its period of pregnancy is fourteen days, and that it broods for fourteen days.
Of birds that live by predation and eat flesh, some have hooked talons, some do not, such as swallows, which feed on the flesh of flies and gnats and the like.
Birds with hooked talons are of various kinds, such as the eagle and the hawk.
The eagle is of seven kinds, such as the mountain eagle, the alforra, the pardella, and other kinds under these.
Of hawks there are sixty-two species, which reduce to four: falcons, goshawks, merlins, and sparrowhawks.
Of falcons there are many species: kestrels, bafarilli, nebularii, sakers, gyrfalcons, and other, lesser kinds, such as picancii, aluari, porcarii, and picarii, and many of this sort.
Goshawks, too, are of many kinds, larger and smaller, such as the noble ones, the buszancii, and others of this sort.
Merlins are of many kinds, and sparrowhawks likewise, such as the noble ones, the ogii, and the tartaram.
The cuckoo belongs to the sparrowhawk family, but has degenerated into a base creature.

It eats the eggs of other birds, such as the fulipe and the like, and lays its own there instead; and its young imitate their father's baseness, for when grown they devour those who reared them, and, driven by necessity, take up their fathers' malice and commit like deeds.

Every bird with hooked talons eats flesh, and we have already completed our account of these in the treatise we composed in our youth for the entertainment of the young royal line, and the Artaham is one of these.
They breed on inaccessible mountains, and for this reason its nest is never found, and no one has seen its young.
Flesh-eating birds breed once a year, except swallows; these alone among flesh-eaters breed twice.
And if the eyes of swallow chicks are injured, they heal and are restored.
The eagle lays three eggs and rears only two of them; and if it rears a third, it casts it from the nest, since feeding several burdens it, and its talons become weak and bent.
Its wings turn white from the burden of its labor, and it broods on its eggs for thirty days.
Other, more moderate birds of prey, such as the hawk, generally brood for twenty days, and if they hatch more chicks than they can rear, they cast the extra ones out.
When they see that their chicks are able to fly, they strike them and drive them from the nest.
Some of these take turns brooding on their eggs, while in others the female broods and the male brings her food.
Black crows do this as well.
The cubeg makes two clutches of eggs, and the female broods on one, the male on the other.
And once they have hatched their chicks, each rears its own.

The peacock lives fifteen years, and begins to breed at the end of its third year, when its feathers take on their color; it broods on its eggs for thirty days, breeds once a year, and lays fifteen eggs. It does not lay every day once it begins, but rests for two or three days, and mates in spring. It sheds its feathers as trees shed their leaves, and when the season returns, those feathers grow back, just as trees first put forth their leaves. And unless watched over while brooding, the eggs are attacked by the males and broken. For this reason many hens flee at this time and hide from their males. And some men place two peacock eggs under a hen, for she could not cover more, given the size of the eggs.

Of fish, some are generated from other fish; some are generated spontaneously from mud and earth. Of those generated from other fish, some are generated by way of seed; some are generated from sweat and surplus matter. Of those generated by way of seed, some are generated from the mating of male and female, some from the female alone. And of the fish generated from the mating of male and female, some generate offspring resembling themselves directly, some lay eggs. And of those that lay eggs, some lay eggs already complete within, and from those eggs generate offspring within; some lay eggs complete outside the body. And these latter are of two kinds, for some of them receive the eggs after they have been fertilized by the males, some do not. And of those that do not receive them, there are two kinds: in some of them the female returns to the eggs, gathers them, and broods over them; in others the female wanders off and does not care for the eggs, and the male gathers the eggs, guards them, and broods over them. And of these eggs, those fertilized by the male hatch, and those not fertilized do not hatch. And of those that are fertilized, some are fertilized more, some less. This classification is known to those with experience, and is gathered from the words of Aristotle.

Of fish, some mate every month and breed accordingly; some every six months; some twice a year; some only once. Some in spring, some in autumn, some in winter, some in summer - and these are the ones that live in the depths of the sea. Some are pregnant for thirty days, some for twenty, some for a single week; some for a month, some even longer, some for less.

Of fish, some generate and give birth to offspring resembling themselves, such as the dolphin and the whale, and some lay eggs.
