Of the egg-layers, some lay eggs already complete within, and generate creatures from them internally, such as the ray; and some lay incomplete eggs externally, and these grow quickly outside, just as the small worms that certain animals generate grow quickly.

Of those that lay incomplete eggs externally, some lay at the bottom of the water, some near the shore, where the water is fresh, in warm places sheltered from wind, and some among rocks; some among the roots of trees and reeds. And when the female lays, the male follows and fertilizes the eggs, and the eggs upon which the seed falls hatch, while the rest do not. Sometimes one male follows the one laying, sometimes many; indeed as many as fourteen males have been seen following a single female.
In some kinds the female returns and broods over the eggs.
In others, the female wanders off, and the male remains and guards the eggs.
A fish of one kind never mates with a fish of another kind.
The eggs of fish are, in some cases, large and few, in others numerous and small.
The formation of the young begins from the head of the egg, and the vessels extend from the heart to the head and eyes.
The upper parts are large at first.
Eggs that are covered by more seed grow faster, especially those of small fish, which sometimes grow in a single day, sometimes in three.
Some fish brood over their eggs for forty days, some for fifty, and these do not reach completion quickly.
Those eggs touched by the seed appear white after one day, and sometimes the eyes appear in them, and afterward the other parts.
What is generated from worms, however, shows the lower parts first, and the eyes afterward.
While fish are small their umbilical cords are extended, and once they have grown these shorten.
The eggs of fish are within a membrane, and within the membrane of the egg is another membrane containing the young.
Between these two membranes is a moisture, which serves as food for the young.
And they are fed through the umbilical cord.
Some have eggs within the womb, such as the fox-shark, a kind of fish, and the tortoise, and small creatures emerge from these, having umbilical cords near the womb.
For this reason some believe that they are in the womb just as other animals are. And some, like the dogfish, bring their young out and then draw them back into themselves again.
The frog, however, does not draw its young back into itself, because of the hardness of its head and spine, as will be said later.
And all fish nourish their young, except frogs.
There is a certain fish that lives both on land and in the sea, called in Greek the rori - the seal.
It breathes and sleeps, and gives birth on land near the sea; most of its life, however, is spent in the sea.
It generates a live young, and the afterbirth comes out with it. Like the sheep, it can give birth at any season, as man does, and bears one, two, or three young.
When its young is twelve days old, it takes it to the sea many times a day, so that it grows accustomed to living in the sea.
It cannot support itself well on its feet. Its flesh is soft, and its bones are cartilaginous, and its voice is like that of a bull.
Fish that live in marshes and rivers are, for the most part, pregnant for five months.
They breed once they are a year old. The dolphin and the whale have milk, and suckle their young, and lie over them while they are small.
Dolphin calves grow quickly. The dolphin is pregnant for ten months, gives birth openly, and lives a long time.
For it has been found that a dolphin lived some thirty years, known by a mark cut into its tail, and was seen thereafter for about thirty years; and another was seen for about twenty years.
The dolphin loves its young greatly, and its calves follow it for a long time.
Some are generated from mud and sand without mating, and none of these have either egg or seed.
This generation occurs in places that dry up.
The mud and decay are stirred, and when the waters return, small fish are generated.
Others are generated from mud and sand, some from mud alone, some from sand alone, and some from the decaying matter that lies on top of the water.
Some fish are called 'foam-fish,' because they are sometimes seen bubbling up in foam, as worms do in dung.
When the year is rainy and warm, many are found, and some are generated from others.
In some there is male and female, yet the female has no eggs, nor the male seed.
And when they are dissected, no passage for seed is found in the male, nor a womb in the female.
Some are generated from mud and rainwater, and some from earth, like earthworms, which are called the intestines of the earth.
And some breed frogs.
The desire for mating, and its pleasure, occurs in all animals, males and females alike, at the season appointed for mating.
Mating itself, and desire for it, is harmful at the time of giving birth.
Males become jealous over their females at the time of mating.
And they become quarrelsome at those times, such as horses and wild boars.
For this reason they rub themselves and go into mud, and afterward dry themselves off, so as to be armored, as it were, for battle, and they fight, and both, or one of them, die.
Rams fight in the same way.
And before this season, all of these move together as one.
But at this season they clash with one another.
The camel and the wolf, too, harm those who approach them at this time.
Wolves and dogs, while nursing their young, are fierce out of jealous protectiveness for them.
Elephants grow wild and destroy houses.
They become fierce at the time of mating.
At this season they flee with their females beyond their usual territory.
At this time there drips from the vulvas of mares the hippomanes, a certain substance resembling dung.
They swish their tails and neigh, and discharge a certain fluid, especially along with their urine.
A horse of two years mates, and the offspring is best from the third year to the twentieth; it mates up to thirty years, the mare up to forty, and the horse begins to mate properly after three years.
They produce good offspring up to twenty years.
The mare becomes pregnant in one day, or two, or three.
Horses and mares desire mating more than other animals, except man.
If a horse is well fed, it mates before the usual season.
The mare produces one or two foals.
The stallion recognizes the mare by scent.
Stallions fight out of jealousy over mares.
The donkey mates after thirty months, and they do not breed until three years, or two and a half.
Cows grow wild, their wombs swell, they leap upon bulls, low, and desire mating excessively, and produce much seed, so much that a single mating fills the cow's womb.
Its mounting is a heavy act.
Old bulls cannot mate many times in one day, but young ones can.
Bulls fight, and the one who wins mounts the cow, and is weakened by the mating.
If it fights afterward with the one it defeated, it is defeated by him, and the one who had been beaten becomes the victor.
And he then mates with the cow.
Bulls mate at one year old, or perhaps after eight months.
The cow carries in the womb for nine months and gives birth in the tenth.
The calf does not survive if born before this time, since its hooves are not yet complete.
She bears one or two.
The bull and cow live fifteen years, and castrated animals live twenty, since excessive mating weakens the body.
Bulls have leaders, as sheep do.
The leaders live longer, on account of good pasture.
The bull sheds its teeth after two years.
They sometimes suffer disease in the feet.
After giving birth, cows have good milk, but before birth they have none.
If the first milk is mixed with water, it curdles and becomes like a stone.
They mate in spring and autumn, and both cow and bull begin mating after two years.
The pig mates after eight months. A one-year-old sow gives birth. In some lands the pig mates after four months, in others after ten, and they continue to breed up to three years.

Domestic pigs become pregnant after eight months and produce up to twenty piglets. If she bears many, she cannot nurse them all, and gives the first teat to the first-born; and a single mating suffices for the sow.
Barley is good food for the mating boar, and cooked barley for the pregnant sow.
Some sows produce good offspring in youth, others later. It is said that if one eye is put out of a pig, it dies.
Pigs live nearly fifteen years. Swineherds appoint leaders among them, calling one of the pigs by its own name, and it goes ahead of the others.

The wild boar mates up to three years old, and what it sires afterward is small-bodied, of little flesh, and poor. A boar with a second sow produces fewer and smaller offspring, and a sow's first litter is small-bodied.
She scarcely gives birth after fifteen years, and because of the strengthened natural heat, those born in winter are better, and those born in summer worse.

When fattened, the pig can mate day and night, and more in the morning, because of the temperance of the blood at that time. It delights in mating out of wantonness rather than from the natural urge to generate.

Sheep in Ethiopia live twelve or thirteen years, and goats thirty-one. Sheep and goats engage in mating throughout their whole lives, and sometimes bear twins if they have suitable food. If they mate facing the north wind, they produce males; if facing the south wind, females. For they should turn their faces toward the north wind when they are to mate.

Goats have no leaders, because of their swiftness. Shepherds say that if old ewes are stirred to mating, it is a good sign, but if young ones are, it bodes ill for them. Ewes bear young up to eight years old, and if well cared for, up to eleven. Rams and goats mate when a year old. The first offspring of goats are the best, which is not so with other animals.
Camels mate from behind, and the female carries in the womb for twelve months and bears one offspring; the male mates after three years, and rests for a year afterward.
The elephant breeds after ten years, and mates after five years, and this in spring; the female carries in the womb for two years, and after giving birth rests for three years.

The dog mates after one year, sometimes after eight months, and the female sometimes becomes pregnant after six months; she does not give birth before sixty days from conception, and can bear young up to eighteen years of age.

Dogs are of many kinds, and dogs breed after a year. The greyhound, that is, the hound, breeds after eight months, and they breed once they reach vigor and begin to lift their leg in urinating; all males lift the leg in urinating after a year, but females crouch down when they urinate.
The greyhound, however, lifts its leg after six or eight months.

Bitches go into heat for seven days, and during this time avoid mating, and the mouths of their wombs swell; after these seven days, they are with dogs for another seven or nine days, and afterward discharge a thick, phlegm-like moisture, and their bodies grow thin after this.

The greyhound bitch carries in the womb for sixty days or a little less, which is a sixth of a year, and her pups are blind for twelve days; and after giving birth, by the sixth month she desires mating again. Some carry for seventy-two days, which is a fifth of a year, and their pups are blind for fourteen days; others carry for three months, and their pups are blind for seventeen days, and are then suckled for another seventeen days, thus thirty-four in all.
Milk is found in bitches four or five days before giving birth, and is thick at first, then becomes thinner. The milk of dogs is thicker than any other milk, except that of pigs and hares.

As bitches approach the age for conceiving, their teats become raised. A bitch generally bears five or six pups, sometimes only one; the greyhound bitch, however, bears eight. Male greyhounds live ten years, females twelve; other dogs live nearly fourteen years, some twenty.
Dogs shed their sharp teeth, called milk-teeth, after four months. Young dogs have white, sharp teeth; old ones, black and blunt.
Here ends the sixth book.

Now something must be said of the lion, which reigns among the other wild beasts. For 'leo' is said to derive from the Greek word for Jupiter in Greece. This animal is so strong that nothing can withstand it except the elephant alone, which Pliny, in his Natural History, says the lion fears.
It is also said that the lion carries in its tail certain herbs which, if a serpent eats them, it dies at once. Likewise, the lion has no voice but the roar, and the lioness none but a growl.

But when the lion and lioness mate, they make no sound at all, but keep silent, so that their cubs will not be detected. Aristotle, however, in his On Animals, says that the lion is a solitary animal.
HERE BEGINS THE NINTH

Having completed, from the beginning of the fifth book up to this point, our account of the operations of animals and their organs that serve the preservation of the species, we shall now take up their operations that serve the regimen of life and the preservation of the individual.
Our discussion of this will extend through these two books, namely the ninth and the tenth, according to this arrangement.
And in these he proceeds as follows: in the ninth he deals with natural behavior and habits, while in the tenth he goes on to voluntary behavior and habits.

This ninth book is divided into two parts: in the first, extending up to the passage 'and the sicknesses of birds are recognized from these,' he treats of the regimen of life; in the second he goes on to the sicknesses that follow from that regimen.
The first part is further subdivided: in the first section, extending from the beginning up to 'and some men hide away in winter,' he deals with regimen as regards nourishment.
In the second he goes on to regimen as regards change of habitation.

The first is subdivided again into two: in the first he deals with the regimen of life among egg-laying creatures, up to 'and the live-bearing quadruped,' and in the second he goes on to the regimen of life among those that bear offspring like themselves.
In the first he proceeds thus: first on swimming creatures, second on flying creatures, third on creeping creatures.

And in this first section he proceeds as follows: first he sets out the differences in the regimen of life among animals in a general way, then he establishes an order among things so as to arrive by this means at the first animal, then he assigns the difference among animals in generation and the concern

for rearing their young; after this he sets out the difference among animals according to place, and takes up his account with those that live in water, and follows through his treatment of these - and so there are four sections, as is evident from the paragraphs.

And he said: 'The nature of the generation of animals is as has been described.' But there is a difference among animals as regards their operations, their regimen of life, their habits and customs, and as regards the affections of the powers of the soul.

And he said: of the affections of the powers of the soul in animals, some are general, some are specific, some are most specific and particular. General ones are, for instance, all the senses, or some of them; specific ones are fear and boldness, anger and lust, which are found clearly in man and in certain animals. Particular ones are, for instance, skills for acting, wisdom for contemplating, and thought for deliberating in men; and in each species of animal certain particular traits are likewise found.

All these affections belong to the side of sensation, and are weakened and impaired by the alteration and impairment of sensation. First come the general ones, then the specific, then the most specific, and they differ by degree. And they become specified and appropriated as nature proceeds by stages, as is apparent to those who observe the ages of man: childhood, youth, manhood, and old age. For in children certain traits resemble the signs of the dispositions that follow later; and yet, in this respect, there is no difference between the soul of a child and that of other animals. They differ once they reach completion, and for this reason the affections of men and of brutes resemble each other at the outset, according to the variation of the senses, to such a degree that the boundaries are hidden and the middle ground unrecognized.

And so it is with other things too, for on this account there is a gradual transition from the inanimate to the animate, proceeding by degrees, and because of the continuity of things the boundaries and the middle ground do not appear, as has been said. For after the inanimate comes first the class of plants, and among plants there are grades; and after that comes the animal. But between the inanimate and the plant, and between the plant and the animal, because of this continuity, the middle ground is scarcely made manifest as to which extreme it more resembles - as appears in the sponge and certain other fixed creatures, such as shellfish and certain leathery-shelled creatures, which, when uprooted from their places, die outright and cannot live. When compared to animals they seem like plants; when compared to plants they seem like animals. And they differ in this: that some of them are wholly without sensation, and some have a weak sensation; and between plants and these there is a certain

difference in motion, in their parts. And this motion likewise varies by degree, and they share a common operation with plants, in that they generate their like - a plant, a plant. In this they are equal; and they share with animals, to a greater or lesser degree, in motion and sensation.

And I say that animals that take pleasure in mating differ in how they give birth to and nourish their young. For some mate, conceive, and give birth at fixed times, and in this they resemble plants. Of these, some are solicitous in procuring food for their young only until they are grown, and afterward abandon them and no longer recognize them at all; and some always recognize them. All animals seek food for their young according to their own nature, from what they themselves naturally delight in; and foods vary according to the variety of the elements from which they are composed.

Of animals, some are aquatic, some are terrestrial, and some share in both, such as those that live on land but whose food is in the water; and many live in the water while their food is on land. Of those living in water, some do not breathe, some do - that is, some take in water through a passage, and some take in air through a lung. And some share in both, such as the dolphin and the whale.

And if one of these falls into a net and is held under water, it will suffocate, but if held out of the water it will live a long time; and these are called swimming creatures, for they take in air to cool the heart, as other land creatures do, and water for food, as other swimming creatures do; and those that take in water have gills, while those that take in moisture as food have a special passage for it. And animals of one species resemble each other in constitution, whether male or female, unless the males are castrated - for a difference in that organ brings about a difference throughout the whole body, and changes it toward the nature of the female.

We divide animals into aquatic and terrestrial for three reasons: because of what they take in, whether air or water; because of the constitution of the body; and because of the food by which they are nourished. And the food taken corresponds to the constitution of the body, and to whether it takes in air or water.

Immobile shelled animals feed on the fresh water that is within the sea, which seeps in through narrow pores - as appears in a wax or earthenware vessel, empty, thrown into the sea with its mouth sealed: if it lies long in the sea and is then taken out and broken open, fresh water will be found inside, which was able to enter through the pores because of its fineness; and some of these creatures feed on small fish.
Aquatic animals that move about and eat other animals feed on small fish, and some feed on plants. No sea creature eats its own young.

After this we shall speak of birds. We say that some birds live on land, some in water, some in watery places and near them, and some at sea and near it. Of those that live in or near water, some have webbing or skin between their toes, such as geese and many others of this kind, and some do not. Of those that live on land, some have hooked talons, some do not; and everything with hooked talons feeds on flesh, such as all the kinds of eagles and hawks - but not everything that feeds on flesh has hooked talons. Of the others that live on land and do not have hooked talons, some feed on grass, some on the seeds of plants, some on both, some on the leaves of trees, some on their fruit, some on both, some on all of these, and some also feed on worms; and of those that live in or near water, some feed on fish, some on frogs, some on both, some even on all of these, and sometimes on plants. In general, all birds drink little, and birds with hooked talons drink almost no water at all, except a few.

Serpents are fond of wine, and eat flesh, and suck the fluids of animals, and spiders do likewise. The venomous asp feeds on whatever it can find, for it eats birds and swallows their eggs whole; and in general serpents can live a long time without food.
On quadrupeds

A live-bearing quadruped, if it is one of the wild kind with unequal, saw-like teeth, eats flesh, as the wolf does, which eats a great deal of flesh at once and then goes two or three days without food, and sometimes eats earth, and for medicinal purposes eats grass and vomits, and is cured, as dogs do. The wolf sometimes eats men, and its breath stinks; for it eats without chewing, and is greedy and slow to digest, drinks little, and its dung is very dry and its urine foul-smelling, and it urinates with its leg raised.

The hyena, the African wolf, has hair on its neck like a horse's mane, and stiff hair on its back over the spine; it deceives men and preys on them, and digs up and devours the buried dead, and imitates human voices, and barks like a dog, deceiving shepherds and devouring their flocks.

The bear eats the fruit of trees, honey, and locusts, and eats all kinds of flesh, once it has let it rot. It fights with stags, cows, and wild boars, and all such creatures drink water by lapping, like the dog and the mouse; those with equal teeth, however, drink by sucking, like the bull.

The pig feeds on roots and many other things, and is fattened quickly in this way: it is given water to drink on the first day, then fed for two, three, or four days, then left fasting for two or three days, then fed again and fattened on barley, millet, husks, and acorns. Old pigs are fattened with mud, and a sixth part of their food goes into bristles and blood and the like. Pregnant sows grow thin because of the nourishment of the young.

The bull feeds on grass and is fattened on gas-producing foods, such as vetch and beans, and on sweet foods, figs, and raisins. If the hide of a bull is pierced and well inflated from within, and it is then fed, it will fatten greatly. The horns of a cow can be bent into any shape with hot wax, warmed. And treatments applied to sore feet with tar, oil, and fish are beneficial.

The horse, mule, and donkey feed on grain and graze on grass. The more the mule and donkey drink water, the more their food benefits them. The horse and camel like to drink muddy water; the cow, however, prefers clear water. Camels live thirty years and more, some a hundred, and can graze for three or four days without water, and then drink a great deal. The elephant lives two or three hundred years, and eats and drinks a great deal.

Sheep and goats eat grass. Sheep graze in flocks, goats scattered about; and sheep are fattened by drinking, and for this reason salt is given to them, both alone and mixed with fodder, to stir up thirst in them.
In autumn they are given gourds with salt to increase their milk, and they are fattened with salt, lentils, and chaff.
And if they abstain from food for three days and are then given it, they fatten greatly.
In summer, cold water from the north benefits them; in autumn, lukewarm water from the south.
Walking at the end of the day and movement along paths benefits sheep, but hard labor harms them.
Sheep that melt the snow or ice that falls on them can withstand the winter.
So do those with a broad tail and abundant wool. But those that do not melt the ice, and that have a long tail and sparse, coarse or curly wool, bear the winter poorly.
Cloth made from the wool of sheep that wolves have killed breeds many lice.
Some men shut themselves in their houses in winter, some in summer; and some move in summer to cold places, and in winter to warm ones.
Some animals that are able to change places do likewise, for, leaving their homes, they flee the winter after the autumn equinox; and some flee the heat after the spring equinox.
They go to places very far off, for fear of the changing air; and cranes fly northward beyond Egypt, where the Nile flows down.
Against them the cubit-tall pygmies wage war, dwelling in cave-like places in those regions.
When cranes move they go in flocks, and grow weary in flight because of the weight of their bodies, and cry out for this reason. In foreign regions they have leaders; in their own, they do not.
Certain other birds, such as the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork, likewise change places, and some flee to the valleys seeking warmth in winter, and in summer to mountaintops seeking coolness.

Fish, too, move from place to place. Some go to the bottom of the sea in winter, seeking warmth, and to the surface of the water in summer, seeking coolness, for light gathers at the bottom of the water and generates heat.
Some come out near the shore for feeding and mild weather, and for this reason their flesh is firmer, while that of those at the bottom of the sea is moister.
Some go to places where rivers flow into the sea, for the food and the freshness of the water there.
Some swim by day and rest at night, unless there is moonlight. Some come out when the water is murky, some when it is clear and bright.
Some hide in summer, some in winter, and for this reason some are worse eating in winter, some in summer.
Some prefer rain, some sunshine; some prefer thin water, some thick.
Some make burrows for themselves in sand, some in mud, and put out only their mouth because of the cold.
Some hide in burrows in summer because of the heat, and some fish renew themselves and shed their old skin and scales, just as serpents shed their skin.
Crabs do this too, and seek suitable places in hollow trees and crevices of rocks, where they remain until their new shell hardens and their scales grow back.
Some shed their skin in this way many times, some only once; and in general rain harms birds, and drought harms fish.

Segmented creatures remain in their burrows in winter because of the cold, and use their stored food sparingly, fearing it will run out; and they emerge thin, and they too renew themselves in old age, and remain hidden in trees and burrows after shedding their skin and casings, as wasps and locusts and creatures of this kind do.
Serpents hide in winter in the earth, and dragons under rocks; toads here and there. Some of these renew themselves and shed their old skin.

Quadrupeds too change places because of cold and heat, and remain in winter in pits and burrows, and some in summer. The bear hibernates, and it is disputed whether this is because of cold or because of heat, since it is very fat at that season; the females give birth then and stay hidden until they emerge with their young, and this happens at the beginning of spring, and they remain hidden for at least forty days. For this reason a pregnant bear is very rarely caught. While hibernating it does not eat, for its intestines are found empty and its stomach without food; and because it hibernates in winter, and is fat while hibernating, this leaves us in doubt whether it does this because of heat or because of cold.
The sicknesses of birds are recognized from their wings, for the position of a bird's wings is disturbed when it is ill.
In fish, sickness is not apparent as it is in men and other animals, except when they grow thin and their color changes.
Some remain at the surface of the water, and the stars harm them.
Especially the rising of the Dog Star, and they then die from the heat.
The heads of fish are afflicted by loud thunder.
The lice that form in the gills of fish kill them.
Ice kills them too.
Drought harms them, especially those with shells.
Rain fattens them, since then they find abundant food.
Rain benefits them by nature, just as it benefits the plants of the earth, for although plants are watered by rivers, wells, or springs, they do not grow as well as with rainwater.
Summer and autumn rain especially benefits fish; yet heavy rain harms them, because of the cold, and because they do not see well then.
Fish are fattened in years that are good for men.
River water also benefits fish.
Deep places suit them, so that some fatten in the depths of the sea, some in green water, and some with a north wind, such as the long fish.
Broad-bodied fish, however, fatten with a south wind.
Fish that have a stone in the head suffer in cold weather, because of the freezing and chill.

Pigs have three sicknesses: an abscess in the ear or in certain other parts, which gradually corrupts the neighboring parts until it reaches the lung; this is a contagious disease, called mange or leprosy of the pig, and it is cured only by cutting away that part. Abscesses of the ears form when the heat is strong and the pigs are heavy. It helps them to eat unripe mulberries, and to be washed thoroughly with water, and to be bled in the veins beneath the tongue.
Another sickness is heaviness of the head, from which most pigs die, and it is cured with strong wine taken through the nostrils. A third sickness is flux, and this perhaps has no remedy.

Pigs afflicted with measles are cured if they drink human urine. Those of soft flesh, with pustules on the leg, neck, or shoulders, under the tongue, or in the armpits, are cured with grains of lupin and chickpeas. Pigs are fattened by a variety of foods and their preparation, and by acorns; yet if pregnant sows eat too many acorns, they miscarry.
Sheep have many sicknesses, nearly all those that afflict men.

Dogs suffer from rabies, which is followed by frenzy; animals bitten by a rabid dog go mad, except man, who dies in full possession of his senses. Quinsy, a sickness of the throat, kills dogs, and gout kills them too.
Cows suffer from gout, which stiffens their feet, but they do not die of it; they die of sciatica and corruption of the lung, whose sign is drooping ears.
The horse suffers from a gout that causes it to shed its hooves, and the sign of it is trembling of the right testicle.
It also suffers from a tightening of the sinews, whose sign is the swelling of the veins of the head and neck, and heaviness in walking.
They suffer from colic, from loss of appetite, and from a rabies whose sign is the drooping of the ears toward the neck, and this sickness has no remedy.
And from blockage of the bladder, so that they cannot urinate.
They also suffer from all the sicknesses that afflict men, and from watery discharges and swellings, and other ailments too numerous to list.
Horses delight in meadows and water, and do not like clear water, so that when they are to drink they stir it up with their hoof; and they like to swim in water.
Donkeys suffer from glanders, when they are afflicted in the head, and hot phlegm flows from the nostrils and descends to the lung, and kills them.
It is a very cold-natured animal, and for this reason it is not found in northern lands.
Wind harms the elephant, causing a bloating sickness because of which it cannot urinate or defecate, and it dies if it eats earth.
It suffers from pain in the joints, against which a drink of warm water and herbs with honey helps.
Its shoulders are anointed with oil and warm water, and it sleeps if it could not sleep before.
It is cured of shoulder pain by applying roasted pork.
It drinks wine, and by drinking oil, iron is drawn out of its stomach.

Segmented creatures grow fat at the time of their breeding, especially if the spring season is warm and moist. Worms that generate spiders harm bees, corrupting their honey. Moths lay their larvae in the honeycombs, and bees fall sick when the flowers swell. Segmented creatures die if anointed with oil and placed in the sun.
Animals differ according to place, for some are found in certain places living long lives, and in others short ones.
The mole, the hare, and ants cannot live in certain lands.
Venomous creatures are not found in certain lands.
The pig is not found in certain others.
Shelled creatures, or shellfish, are large in the Red Sea.
In Theoria, sheep have broad tails a cubit long.
And the goat has ears a palm's length.
In certain lands, bulls have hair on their shoulders like the camel.
In certain others, goats are shorn, like sheep.
In Libya, rams and sheep have horns.
In the north, rams lack horns.
In Egypt, bulls and sheep are very large.
Dogs and wolves, hares and foxes, crows and hawks, however, are small.
In some places this variation comes from the constitution of the region.
In others, from the scarcity or abundance of food.
In some places small birds are not found, because of the harshness of winter.
A lizard longer than a cubit is found in Arabia.
In Libya a kind of serpent is found that has no width.
In some lands wolves are numerous.

And they vary because of habituation, and because of the crossbreeding of one kind with another, as of the donkey and the mare, the wolf and the dog, and because of the variety of places, such as mountains and valleys.
Some things are opposed to others, as the saliva of man is to venomous creatures.
Some animals, with their bite, cause to rot or to burn whatever they have bitten.

They also differ in many other respects: in softness and hardness, in fertility and sterility, in quality, color, youth and old age - for in general, old fish are poor both for salting and for eating.
In general, males are better than females.
River and lake fish are good after spawning.
Some are poor at the time of spawning.
They vary in these respects and many others too long to list.
And here ends the ninth.

We have now completed our account of the natural behavior and habits of animals, and it remains for us to complete our discussion of their voluntary behavior and habits. We shall first establish the truth about the friendship and enmity of animals, and then go on to the intelligence and learned skill that arises in them - first concerning blooded animals, and after that concerning the bloodless, segmented ones. We shall first set out some general points, then descend to particulars.

And Aristotle said: 'Our knowledge of small, short-lived animals is slight, but of the large and long-lived we know somewhat more' - especially in those in which knowledge, character, and other affections of the soul are found. We observe that some learn from others, some from men, especially those with good hearing, by which sounds are recognized, and perfect senses, by which sensible things are perceived.

We also observe that in all kinds of animals in which sex is distinguishable, the female is more easily trained than the male. Females are sharper and more attentive toward the fruit of their womb than the males are, and they are also weaker, except perhaps in those that live by predation - though mares are duller than horses, more prone to anger and less tame. This is manifest in man too, as an example: for woman is more easily swayed, loves more, has a stronger memory, is more quickly deceived, lies more readily, quarrels more often, and is of greater malice and lesser hope. Man, however, is bolder, of greater usefulness, and quicker in movement.
As for enmity and friendship among animals, we know that among quadrupeds the cause is food, territory, jealousy over mating, and teaching and incitement.

Flesh-eaters fight with all creatures, or with those on which they feed, as do birds with hooked talons and predatory quadrupeds, such as the wolf, the bear, and the lion, against bulls, horses and donkeys, sheep and goats, and the other creatures they feed on. Those that feed on the same prey fight each other too, especially when food is scarce. This is the cause of the fighting between the vulture and the dragon, between dogs and crows, between crows and kites, and among all creatures of this kind. For this reason the owl fights the crow: the owl hunts by night, and the crow, stronger by day. The owl devours the crow's eggs, and the crow the owl's.

Some also fight over territory, and drive each other off out of rivalry, or because the place cannot hold them both, or because some hinder others in gathering their food. For this reason the ibis fights the horse: the horse begrudges the ibis its place, drives it from the pasture, and eats the grass; the ibis, for its part, suspects it will lose the frogs, which flee when the horse walks through the meadow, and so it flies over the horse and startles it, forcing it to flee.

Some fight against others out of jealousy over mating. This fighting is evident among horses, bulls, wolves, dogs, and pigs, and certain other animals, and even among men. For this reason the elephant attacks men at the time of its mating; it knocks down walls with its shoulders and trees with its forehead.

From training and incitement, dogs fight each other and other animals. From this too, a domesticated elephant fights against a wild one, being commanded and incited to fight against it, and it will strike it until it obeys. The domesticated one, being better fed, is stronger, and once it has overcome the other, the hunter, riding the domesticated one, leaps upon the wild one and binds it.

Animals love one another and form the firmest friendships, and some gather together, such as those of one species. Of these, some go about two by two, like turtledoves and others of this kind, and some together in a herd, like cranes, doves, sheep, cattle, pigs, and goats; and if separated from one another they perish from fear - as a pregnant ewe, left alone, will miscarry from fear if she hears thunder. Cows, too, are lost if separated from the herd, since they do not dare to defend themselves and are eaten by wild beasts.

Among those of one species, some love their own kind remarkably, as horses do: if a mare dies and leaves a foal, another mare, though barren, will take it in, but since she has no milk, the foal dies. Sheep, too, love one another, though not as much. Some even love one another though not of the same species, as the crow and the fox. And creatures that feed on the same things, if that food becomes overabundant, become tame through this very abundance of food, as is seen in Egypt, where there is a great abundance of food for animals.

Animals have intelligence, as the stag does, which out of prudence grazes near a road, where other animals do not come close, because of men; and out of prudence it takes turns between grazing and suckling its young, and places its offspring in crevices of rocks, so that if need be it can fight well and defend itself and its young.

When a stag is being fattened, or when it has shed its antlers, it hides out of prudence, since it could not defend itself then; it hides by day among trees where there is grass, because of the wolves it flees, and grazes by night until its antlers grow back.

Out of prudence it dries its antlers in the heat of the sun, and rubs them against trees to harden them. Its antlers grow in this way: at one year small antlers appear; at two years the antlers emerge like plowshares; in the third year they grow and branch into two; in the fourth they thicken. And so they increase up to six years.
After this many branches grow, and from that time on it is not known how old they are. Old stags, however, do not have small teeth, nor antlers that curve forward.

Stags delight in song, and are killed by this means, for while some sing to them, another strikes and kills them. Out of prudence they eat dragon-wort, and chew it with the tongue to sharpen their teeth. Out of prudence, wild goats in Crete, when wounded by an arrow, seek out dittany, with which they draw it out.
Dogs, when sick, eat roots and grasses in order to vomit and be cured; and some, if they sense they have eaten poison, seek out human dung, by eating which they escape the danger.
In Egypt, stags bellow for help against serpents, and roll themselves in mud, so as to armor themselves against them, as it were. Some open their mouths and offer their teeth to birds, to be cleaned.

The tortoise, after devouring a viper, eats wild marjoram. Weasels fight with serpents, which they eat, and after the fight run to rue, which is harmful to serpents. Hedgehogs, out of prudence, dig burrows facing away from the winds, and there are many things of this kind.

Intelligence shines forth in birds too, for by it a certain bird, the weasel-bird, prepares mud with straw, or ash with water; and when it builds the walls of its dwelling it places the harder material in the foundation, and after breeding it casts the droppings of its young out of the nest, and even teaches its young to do this once they have grown.
Doves keep the laws of marriage, for the male, unless he has lost his mate, does not go to another, nor does the female submit to another, unless she has lost the first.

The male strikes the female if she is slow to come to the young, and he teaches them to eat and to mate, for he brings salted earth and places it in the mouths of the chicks; and before he drives them out, he mates with them.
Turtledoves, having lost their mates, do not take a second.
Turtledoves and doves live and breed for fifteen years.
In general, male birds live longer than females, except among turtledoves, whose males die first.
Among sparrows, males live only one year, while females live long.
Large, heavy birds, out of prudence, build their nests in pine trees, so as to escape by this means the onslaught of eagles and hawks.

It is a marvel concerning the partridge, which flies around the hunter so that, while he tries to catch her, her chicks may flee; and many other birds do likewise, flying around men so that, while they try to catch them, they may draw them away from their nests or their young.

Some hide their eggs from their own males, since the males break their eggs through mating, as peacocks do; and some have remarkable cunning and sharp intelligence, coming secretly to their females out of jealousy of other males; and out of the prudence by which they love worms, they bore into trees to get at them.

And if someone places an almond or a nut in those holes so that they sprout and close up the holes, these birds bore into the fruit and draw out what is inside, so as to destroy its power to germinate.

Cranes, out of prudence, when they move from place to place, rise up high so as to survey the most distant places to which they are going. And as the cranes rest, standing on one foot, sleeping with their heads lowered under their wings, only their leader raises its head, keeping watch from afar, so that, if it sees anything, it may cry out, waking the sleepers from their slumber.
Out of prudence some nest in inaccessible places, or in hollow trees, or in crevices of rocks, for the safety of their young.

Since nature does not fail in what is necessary, it gave webbing between the toes to birds that dwell on the seashore or on the banks of rivers and lakes, and swim by this means; and they show remarkable intelligence in nesting and rearing their young. Others, with rigid toes, show sharp intelligence in this too. Some nest on mountains, some in cities; and of those in cities, some nest atop houses, some inside houses, some outside under the eaves. And of those that nest on mountains, some nest in trees, some in holes in trees, some in crevices of rocks, some within cone-shaped mounds of earth. Some build nests of mud, some of straw, some of twigs, some even of aromatic substances, such as cinnamon and the like.
They line their little nests and the bedding of their young, some with wool, some with the bristles and hair of animals, human hair, or the down of trees.

Some lay eggs within the hide of a hare or a fox, until they break and the young come out. All this comes from a remarkable intelligence and subtle cunning, by which they procure what is fitting for themselves and their young, and avoid harm.

They are of various species, and some, within a single species, come in different varieties, as vultures do, which are of many kinds, of which the first nests in places with many trees, and sometimes near cities, and flies near mountains in search of food.

There is another kind, smaller in size and strength than the first, dwelling in mountains and desert places. There is a third, smaller in size and vigor than the first two, black in color, which kills hares and feeds itself and its young on them.

There is a fourth kind of vulture, with poor and very small wings, white-headed, of middling size among the other vultures, dwelling in places with many trees, of no strength at all, so that crows overcome and drive it off, and it is of a perverse and troublesome disposition, always hungry and screeching.
There is a fifth kind of vulture, thick-necked and twisted, broad-chested, dwelling on the seashore; what it catches it carries out to sea and devours there.
There is a sixth kind of vulture, six times the size of the other vultures, with a strong cry, yellowish in color, and this is the true vulture.
Others are of mixed kind, or born of a vulture or a hawk with other birds.
The vulture hunts from midday until night, and rests from sunrise until midday.
As it grows old its beak lengthens and sharpens.
And because it happens that it dies of hunger in the end, it is fabled of it that it was once a man who did harm to travelers.
From what remains of its food it feeds its young, and brings it down to them with beak and talons, and nests in high places and in trees.

It feeds its young until they can fly, and afterward does not allow them to come near the nest, since it cannot support them, and out of resentment, when its young are being fattened, it casts them out before their time.
And a certain bird feeds them.
Vultures fight one another over territory, dwelling place, and food.
The vulture hunts in places very far from its nest, and perches high up so as to rise more easily, and in flight climbs very high so as to see distant places.
For this reason it is called the bird of god.
It hunts hares and foxes, and fawns, and other creatures of this kind.
And it lives a long time.
A certain bird, called in Greek makom, is of keen sight, and forces its young to fix their gaze upon the disk of the sun, and kills the one whose eyes water.
And it feeds the others on birds that live by the sea.
And if it sees a vulture, out of fear it plunges itself into the water.
The vulture, however, flies above it until it is forced to surface, and when it comes up, seizes it.

Sparrowhawks are of three kinds, and differ in this: some of them seize doves resting on the ground, but if the doves fly, they do not attack them; others seize doves if they perch in trees, but not if on the ground or in the air; a third kind catches them while they fly, but does not approach them on the ground or in a high place. And it is said that doves recognize them, so that if they are of the kind that catches in the air, the doves come down to the ground; if of the kind that catches on the ground, the doves fly. And some of these sparrowhawks come down among the birds at the call of men; and the birds, out of fear of them, fall and are caught. These accept what is thrown to them, though they are untamed and wild; and once they have eaten, they withdraw, and the next day return at the call of men.
On falcons

As for the intelligence of falcons, goshawks, and merlins, those experienced in these matters say that they know their masters, and are trained to kiss them and to wipe their beaks on their cheeks and beards, and recognize the voices of those accustomed to calling them; and they have returned from the most distant places to their masters' homes. The eagle, out of prudence, allows hawks to tire themselves out hunting, and then suddenly swoops down and strikes them; and when the eagle sees that they cannot hide, because the place is clear of trees and rock crevices, it does not wait for them to tire. Such is the way of birds.
On sea creatures
Sea creatures are of great cunning and sharp intelligence in feeding themselves and their young, and also in fighting against adversaries.
They have many of the same cunning tricks and habits as are found in birds.
Many men have said of a certain kind of frog that it has, above its eyes, something like long hairs, certain appendages by which it stirs up mud and sand.
And a fish gets entangled and is drawn toward these.
And they seek, beneath weeds and in green water, small fish on which they feed.
A certain kind of frog feeds on foam, and out of prudence opens its mouth against the current of the water, and gathers flies and gnats in its jaws as if in a net.
Crabs, out of cunning, insert small stones between the shells of an oyster, and feed on its flesh.

Some, with deliberate skill, cut through the net with their teeth, and out of a kind of loyalty run through the nets and lead all the fish out through those holes, so that the others escape first, and only afterward do they themselves come out.
And if the threads of the net are strong, many gather together and chew and cut through them.
Out of prudence some guard their eggs and fight against an adversary, and once they have driven it off, return to their places, lay their eggs again, and brood over them.

Some make a clattering noise with their jaws and teeth to drive off their adversaries, and out of prudence change their location according to the different seasons, from the bottom of the water to the surface, and from the surface back down to its depths.
And some fish cover themselves with weeds and mud so as not to be seen, and so hunt better,
and some fight by ambush too, and form ranks, and band together, and bite their adversaries.

Some, out of prudence, press close to the earth and rocks, since they take on their color, and they do this sometimes out of fear, so as not to be seen by their adversaries, sometimes out of another kind of cunning, so as to leap unexpectedly upon those they intend to devour.
Some turn themselves upside down so as to be carried by the wind, as if by a sail, by means of their shells or the thin webbing between their digits.
It is a matter of doubt whether the shells of shellfish could be removed without their death and destruction.
It is also doubted whether the generation and growth of shells comes from seed or from surplus matter.

Among segmented creatures there are many of great industry and remarkable intelligence, such as the kinds of ants, spiders, bees, and wasps. For ants proceed along a single path, store up food for themselves, and know how to castrate grain and destroy its power to germinate. They do not shirk the work of the task. All those in one anthill recognize each other and help one another against an adversary. They cut off the legs of worms so that they cannot flee from them, and they labor at night when the moon is full.

The kinds of spiders are many: one is small, of varied color; another is larger, black in color. The first is further subdivided into many kinds, one of which is small and builds no web at all. There is another, larger than this, which builds a rough web near the ground in holes, and, standing in that web, watches until some small creature falls, upon which it leaps and catches it.

After this there is a fourth kind, more skilled in its webs and its hunting, for once the web is made it stretches out its edges like the cords of a tent, and weaves a sufficient web in the middle, and stands watching in the middle itself; and its sense is remarkable, for when a small creature falls into that net it easily feels it, and binds and wraps the web until it has entangled it, then carries it off and stores it in a suitable place, and when hungry sucks its moisture; and if the web is torn in some part, it repairs it at once before beginning to hunt again.

It hunts for the most part at sunrise and sunset. The female gives birth, and hunts, and the male assists her. The female loves her little spiders greatly, for if anyone touches them with anything, the mother immediately runs up and bites that thing, as if driving it away from her young; and when she moves from place to place she carries them all together upon herself, so that she looks like a loaded cart; and if anyone touches her with something, the young at once fall off and scatter, and she stands and waits for them until they gather together and climb back onto her.

After these there are two other kinds, one larger, one smaller. The larger has long legs, and, so as not to be seen, hangs beneath its web and hunts. The smaller stretches out its web and hides within it, catching the small creatures that fall into it.
It is clear that spiders sometimes hunt large creatures, so much so that they will weave a web over a small lizard and bind it with a strong wrapping, then bite it until it dies.
On bees
After these come other segmented creatures that build dwellings out of wax or a similar sticky substance, and there are nine kinds, six of which gather in swarms: these are bees, wasps, and hornets.
Of bees I say first that their kinds are many, for there is a certain kind of bee that is small, round, dense in body and compact - and this kind is dull.
There is another kind whose bees are elongated, though still small.
There is a third kind whose bees are large, broad in the belly.
There is a fourth, whose bees are larger than all those mentioned, heavy and troublesome, lacking a stinger.
Abenfarag says that the smaller the body of the bee, the greater its vigor and the better its work.
There are two other kinds of bees that do not make honey.
One of these neither makes honey nor helps to build the dwellings, but spoils the work of the other bees.

All these kinds differ according to two distinctions, for those born of bees fed on garden flowers differ from those that feed on mountain flowers, since the mountain bees are smaller in body, stronger, and more industrious.

Bees have males, and the males lack stingers, though they pretend they wish to sting with a stinger, and they grow insolent if they have nothing to fear, for if their leader dies, the males mix with the females inside the hives.
And they occupy many of the bees' cells, and often build cells for themselves.
But if the leader is alive, the males are kept separate in one part by themselves, since the leaders keep them in order and punish their excesses.
The leaders of bees are of two kinds.
The better of them is reddish, the other black.
The female leader is beautiful, and twice as large as an ordinary bee.
After this let us take up our discussion of the operations of bees with care.
It is not easy to determine exactly how and in what way they gather and assemble wax and honey.
Yet we report as we have learned it from those who came before us, and as it is confirmed to us by those who, through long attentiveness to bees, have become experienced in these matters.
They gather wax from the flowers of various trees and from olive leaves, and collect it on their front legs, then carry it to their middle legs, and afterward to their haunches.
Because of the weight of the wax they do not range widely among the flowers, but gather in one place what they need.
And then they carry it to the hives.
They build their cells like little vessels, and one cell has two openings, like two vessels sharing one base.
One entrance is on the inner side, the other on the outer.
The openings between the combs and the cells are small, and there are two or three passages between them.
Some cells are entirely filled with wax.

Around the hive, at the edge of the entrance, they deposit a very dark residue that comes from the wax, of sharp odor, which is good for ripening boils and abscesses; and from this residue, and from the wax, comes an oil weaker than this residue itself.
When they build these cells described above, the bees are assigned to their tasks, for some carry the wax.
Some soften it.
Some bring water, and they first build the wax cells in which the bees themselves live, and afterward the cells of the leaders and the males.
They begin building from the top of the hive down to its base.
And from the flowers of oaks, willows, and other trees they bring something sweet, like a sticky fig-substance, and smear it over the surface of the hive, so that no entrance is left open
to harmful creatures.
Once the cells have been prepared, they gather honey from clean stones, leaves, and the flowers of trees, upon which it descends at night, like dew.
There are some places where men themselves can gather the honey that descends from the air onto flowers and leaves, and when they put it on the tongue they taste its sweetness.
Simple folk have called this manna.
Bees, then, feed on honey, and love and guard it exceedingly.

When the hives are robbed and the bees return and discover the theft, out of the devotion they have for their honey, they eat excessively of what remains, and eat also the sticky sweet substance mentioned above.
They eat grapes, figs, cooked wheat, meat, and many things of this kind in which they perceive sweetness.
And this is their food.

Bees have other tasks as well. Let us touch on each of these. First, on the task of the leaders, or kings. We say, then, that among bees there are kings, and they lack stingers. They love and guard their bees to such a degree that if any young bee is left behind somewhere, the king himself goes to seek it, and detects it by scent, and brings it back to the hive.

He himself goes out and comes in ahead of the bees. He directs and corrects the excesses of the bees and of the males. And he never appears outside alone, but only with a great army of bees; he is in the middle, and the bees are all around him.
The king's departure comes three days before the departure of the young bees. Afterward a few bees go out, and the young gather together and separate, so that each king goes off with his own swarm.

And if it should happen that one part of the bees goes off in a different direction, the small remaining part goes to the wealthier king, and abandons its own, on account of whose wickedness and negligence the others left.

If the abandoned king pursues them to bring them back, they turn and kill him. Bees are faithful, however, to a good king and a diligent leader, for if the king grows old and can no longer fly, the swarm of bees will carry him, and if he dies, they die too.

All bees, king and lowliest alike, are attentive to their honey and their young, and for this reason they fight against anyone who takes the honey from them, and sting him, and kill the bees that do not make honey and cast them out of the hive; and they kill their leaders, especially those who hold the place of captains, and kill other small creatures that harm them, and sometimes large animals too, such as horses and cows - indeed they have already killed a horse. They sting only once, for the intestine comes out with the stinger, and they die from this, since they cannot draw the stinger out of the wound without the intestine remaining attached to it.

Bees are helped by, and recognize, their keepers who have long been experienced with them. They clean their cells of dead bees and other filth, and they defecate while flying, for their dung has a strong stench and its foulness distresses them. Strong, young bees make hard honey, and do not sting as forcefully as old ones; old bees are tough, young ones soft. Honey gathered in spring is cleaner, sweeter, and better than autumn honey. Honey is better in new wax; in old wax the honey is reddish and spoiled, as wine spoils in old skins.

Honey that resembles gold is good; pale honey is not as good. Pale honey is effective for eye ailments and for boils. The best honey is at the bottom, as wine is best in the middle, and oil at the top. Honey, whether abundant or scarce, brings idle and old bees back to work.

Bees die from many causes: from harm inflicted from without and from harm arising within. From harm inflicted from without: this comes from moths, and from certain birds, from toads and frogs that dwell in foul places, and from spiders and certain others. From harm arising within: this comes from sicknesses that befall them, one of which arises from over-fertile hives, whose very fertility suffocates and kills them. They also die quickly from inactivity, from the stench of the hives, and from small worms found at the bottom of the hive from decay. They die too from an excess of leaders. And from harm they bring on themselves, they die from gluttony and anger, when they eat too much, and from stinging.
On wasps
Wasps are of two kinds: some are wild, and breed in trees on mountains, and are long, black, and strong-bodied; their stinger is large and stings forcefully. This kind is of two varieties.

Domestic wasps are likewise of two varieties, and breed in the ground, digging and removing earth, as ants do. Some have a stinger, some do not; some are male, some female; and the males have no stingers, as with bees.
Wasps have leaders, and the leaders have a stinger, but do not sting as forcefully as the leaders of bees.

Some build many large nests or combs, some few and small. Some make their nests or combs of wax, some of mud and earth. In one nest they make four openings or more, and breed at least twice a year, and have only one leader per nest, though bees may have several leaders in one hive.

Some die in winter, chiefly because they do not store up food, as bees do. Men are uncertain about the death of wasps, and about many other things concerning them. The food of wasps is flowers and fruit, and especially flesh, and for this reason some nest in graves and some near dung.
And since we detest them, we do not wish to speak further of them.
After this let us speak of another kind of difference among animals, according to boldness and fear, gentleness and fury, which are found in domestic and wild animals alike.
We say, then, that the wolf is bold, and so does not flee or fear when it sees hunters.
If it sees many closing in on it, it withdraws slowly, looking behind it, and when it must flee, it runs like a dog.
If it comes upon an animal while fleeing, it leaps upon it.
It can be tamed easily, and will follow those who have raised it, and will love them and wish to play with them.
And it hates those who do it harm.

So, if it is stoned, it will kill, if it can, the one who threw the first stone at it, whether or not that stone actually harmed it; if it did not harm it, it will nonetheless attack him, since he showed others the way to stone it.
And if it can, it will harm him with its claws, though only slightly.
It is vicious over food, especially if hungry.
Old wolves are very dangerous.
For they come near cities and eat men, since age no longer allows them to hunt, nor do they have sharp teeth as they did when young.
Wounds from the bites of wolves are dangerous, and are treated with the same remedies used for the bite of a rabid dog.
A sponge should be applied with bandages, to draw out the venom and cleanse the wound.
Wolves are of two kinds, one stocky, the other lean, with coarse fur and a bolder temperament.
Wolves have strong heads.
Wounds on them become infected easily.

There are many animals that differ according to these dispositions, for some love men and neither fear nor flee them, nor do men fear them; and some fear men, and defecate out of fear. And there is a marvel among these animals, for when a female of them is about to give birth, many others of that species gather and pile up dung around her, placing it like a wall, so that she may hide within it.

The elephant is said to be the most tamable of all animals, and takes instruction best, so that it is even trained to bow before a king. It is stirred by the color red. It has great jealousy at the time of mating. It is bold, and of good sense among animals, and it is said to foresee rainy and wintry weather in advance.

Horses recognize their mothers, and so do not mate with them, and for this reason a certain horse killed the man who arranged it, because he had covered its face so that it would mate with its own mother. Another horse threw itself from a height and killed itself, upon realizing it had mated with its mother. And there was another that bit off its own testicles and genitals, because its face was uncovered before it had finished mounting its mother. Horses are strong-willed creatures: some have recognized their masters and fought for them against an adversary; some have wept at the death of their masters; and some refused to eat after their death, and died.

Sea creatures too have a remarkable way of showing these dispositions, for many dolphins have companions, and when one dies, the others carry it upon themselves, guarding it so that it will not be eaten by other fish.
They try to draw the harpoon out of a wounded companion, and if they cannot, they flee out of fear.
Animals perform various actions, and change them, and even the shape of certain organs, as happens with roosters, which sometimes kill their hens.

They themselves show concern for the feeding of their chicks. Certain hens, having defeated roosters, raise up their necks and breasts and leap upon the roosters and crow as they do, and combs grow on them.

In short, castrated animals change in certain features of their form, as appears in man: if he is castrated before reaching the age of producing seed, hair does not grow in the places where it should; and if castrated afterward, it does not grow in the same way, nor will it grow further, except the hair of the pubic region.
The voices of castrated animals change to resemble those of females. And if they are castrated in youth, they grow larger.

Stags do not grow antlers if they are castrated before the antlers first appear; and if castrated afterward, the antlers do not grow further, nor do the stags shed them. After castration, animals do not breed.
Here ends the tenth.

Let the reader of this our translation know that from the beginning of this book we have, for the most part, followed in summary the words of Antecer and his arrangement, though in a few places we have proceeded according to Abenfarag and the glosses on Antecer and Abenfarag. And according to our own understanding we have arranged one alongside the other, following the bounds and limits set by the foremost philosopher. It is our intention and purpose, however, from here to the end of the book, to continue for the most part according to the arrangement and sense of the wise and venerable judge Averroes.

And he said: 'Aristotle's intention in this book is to set out the methods and dialectical procedures suited to our inquiry into animals, since the general dialectical procedures applicable to everything are given in the Book of Demonstrations, while those proper to this science are fitted to it specifically. And what Aristotle sets out in this book is gathered into three questions, to which he prefaces a prologue. The first of these is how many causes are sought in this science, and how they compare to one another. The second is how necessity is found in natural things, and what proportion applies to them. The third is what methods there are for knowing the matters gathered in this science, and the procedures for this demonstration.'

Here follows Aristotle's prologue. He said: 'In every reasoned undertaking there are two ways of arriving at certainty: one is to know the questions at issue in that undertaking, the other is to know the particular principles by which the practitioner operates in that undertaking, so that he may judge what has been said in it, where it is true and where it is mistaken.' For this reason it is right that the practitioner should possess this competence before he begins to work. And for this it is necessary that in every undertaking the definitions and terms of the causes be known, the propositions enumerated, and the arrangements understood. And it is necessary that these things be known to anyone wishing to undertake any work, before he begins, and each of them requires its own consideration.

The first inquiry. It is clear that it is necessary for the master of this science to take as given what appears to the senses in each kind of animal and in each species of them, and to inquire into the four causes, which are these: that on account of which, which is the final cause; that by which, which is the efficient cause; that from which, which is the material cause; and the fourth, which is the property and nature, and is the formal cause.

For we would not know perfectly what flesh is unless we knew its nature, and what it is made from, and by what, and for what it is found in the animal - and likewise in mechanical and artificial things. Yet Aristotle says that the carpenter sees his craft's principle more readily than the natural philosopher sees his.

The wise men of old recognized, of these four causes, only the efficient and the material; hence Empedocles said that the four elements are the material cause, and love and hatred the efficient cause. And Anaxagoras says that the boundless mixture - that is, matter - is the material cause, and the intellect that knows is the efficient cause; but the formal and final causes they never understood, until Socrates, as Aristotle said.

For they believed that form and end necessarily followed upon matter, and they gave as an example the fact that bones are found in the animal because earthy elements necessarily sink and gather together, while watery elements rise and solidify above.
And they did not understand that the form of bones, flesh, and skin arises from the purpose of generation.

It is clear that this view of theirs is mistaken. Matter exists for the sake of form, and is posterior to it in generation, for it is the same in natural things as in artificial ones: just as stones and bricks are found for the sake of the form of a house, so the homogeneous parts exist for the sake of the heterogeneous ones.
And the heterogeneous parts are found in order to complete the form of man, who is an embodied spirit.

And just as the form of a house precedes it in time and in nature within the mind of the builder, so the form of man precedes, in time and in definition, the being of individual men, since man is generated only from man, and horse only from horse; hence there must necessarily be an efficient power in the seed - its form is the seed - and if form merely accompanied matter, it would not be an efficient cause at all, and the world would then follow from mere chance.

And since the existence of man and of the animal, and of any of its organs, is for the sake of nature, it is clear that it does not suffice for one who wishes to know the nature of bone, flesh, face, hand, and foot merely to say what things they are made from - that is, fire and earth - but it is necessary to say, for each of these, what it is, and by what power it was generated as such.
Just as, in artificial things, it does not suffice for the craftsman to know what a bed is made from, but he must also know the proper form and shape of a bed.

And since natural things exist for the sake of nature, and nature is predicated both of form and of matter, it is clear that whoever wishes to examine natural things must first know that nature which is predicated of form, since this nature is predicated primarily of form and only secondarily of matter.
And the natural philosopher needs to examine matter, but all the more so, form.

It does not suffice for the master of this science to know the outward shape that presents itself to the senses in an animal; he must also know the particular power belonging to that shape by which the species performs its proper function - for a man of stone and a natural man are one in shape, and likewise a hand of linen and a natural hand.

Man and hand are said of these only equivocally, and in the same way living and dead are said equivocally; hence, since this is so, the master of natural science is said to examine the spirit, since the spirit is a form posterior to the animal's body.

And he must know the four causes of this spirit - material, efficient, final, and formal - and know whether this spirit is one, and the nature by which it is one, and the nature by which it is divided into many parts.

It is clear that not every motion belongs to one and the same spirit, for the spirit that is the principle of generation and creation is not the spirit that is the principle of sensory motion; and the rational spirit, which is the natural spirit proper to man, by which man is naturally distinct from brutes, is more distinct still. Beyond this comes the separable intellect.

It is fitting, then, that the master of natural science should know the nature of the spirit in a general way, and after this the nature of each of its parts, according to what is proper to each part; and it is clear that the formal cause is found in these, since natures do not act as they act except for the sake of something notable, just as a craft does not operate except for the sake of something.

And if nature did not act for the sake of something, everything would come about by chance, and there would be no efficient cause at all; and the discovery of this cause appears more clearly in the heavenly bodies than in corruptible ones, since nothing in the heavens appears idle, as things do among these lower things - and for this reason, whoever said that the heavenly bodies are idle and the product of chance erred more gravely than one who said this of these other, lower things.
What has been said, then, of the causes and their relations to one another, is sufficient.

The second inquiry. I say that whatever exists by nature exists through one of these two: either it was for the sake of something notable and deliberate, or it exists because of the power of matter - for example, breathing, which necessarily follows upon every blooded, mobile animal.

And this statement - namely, necessity - is said in two ways: one concerns those things that follow upon an animal from the necessity of matter, such as death and weakness from old age, and everything else without which an animal cannot exist; the other is the relation of the three causes to the final cause, for if the final cause is found, or is apt to be found, the efficient cause, the matter, and the form must necessarily be found too.

And there are cases in which the end and the form differ in kind and in nature: for there are some things in which the form itself is the very end - for example, if a house is found, matter and a builder must necessarily be found too, but not the reverse, since a builder and matter may be found without a house therefore being found.
This matter is treated in the second book of On Generation and Corruption.

Therefore, whatever is found in an animal exists in one of these three ways: either it is found for the sake of an end, and the end cannot exist without it, as sight cannot exist without an eye; or it is found so that the end may be better, though the end itself could exist without it - as the doubling, or pairing, of the sensory organs; and there are many other things found in an animal without which the animal could still exist, but it is better with them - for a single eye or a single ear would suffice for the animal's completeness, but it is better, and its preservation is greater, because of the excellence of these paired organs; or it is found because of the necessity of matter, such as the excretion of the body's surplus matter, and the growth of hair, and certain other things that follow upon matter. This last is the position held by the ancients, who said that everything existed for the sake of matter alone, and who did not understand the final cause - and this was the greatest ignorance, for they did not recognize the skillful workmanship of nature.

For we see that nature, even from those things that follow upon matter, draws some advantage precisely because they follow it - as appears in bile, which, because it follows matter, irritates the belly and brings on the discharge of waste; and black bile produces appetite. This is enough concerning how many ways necessity, or the necessary, can be spoken of in the science of animals.

The third inquiry, which requires subtle investigation, since it is very difficult to know the method by which the master of this science should proceed in ordering his divisions and in fixing the number of the kinds of animals.

And they judged that the way to this is one of two: one is the way of the arithmetician and the geometer - namely, the way of dividing intelligibly and of enumerating in a general and common manner, and this way suffices in arithmetic and geometry to enumerate their kinds; the other is the way followed by the master of astronomy in enumerating the kinds he derives from the senses, since the way to enumerate the kinds in this science is through the senses - either because he himself perceives them, or because he trusts another who perceived them, if his own life does not last long enough for him to perceive the whole, as Ptolemy did, who set down the kinds that he himself observed and that Hipparchus and certain others before him had observed.
And according to this method he completed his book.

And whoever examines these two ways thoroughly will conclude entirely that neither suffices by itself in this science of animals, to enumerate its kinds and arrange them in a natural order - for if one follows the way of the senses, one will not grasp where the most specific species lie; and if one wishes to speak of each species individually and show its properties and causes, one will have to repeat the same things many times over, and also because some things are equivocal across many most specific species.

And also because the differences used to establish these will be neither primary nor natural, and also because it is not in man's nature to grasp by sense all the most specific species of animal, as the astronomer was able to grasp by sense in astronomy.

And the way of division used in arithmetic and geometry, although it shows the equivocal terms first and the proper ones afterward, does not suffice in the science of animals, as Aristotle said, since it cannot reach the most specific species of animal, in the way that this same method reaches the most specific species in arithmetic and geometry.

And if there were a division that divided a genus by two opposite differences, and each of these in the same way by two further ones, and so on descending, as in arithmetic and geometry, this could not work, since in the science of animals many differences are found within a single species.
