And since only one difference is proper and the others are superfluous, whoever wishes to proceed in this way in the science of animals, so as to reach the ultimate species, will fall into one of these four errors.

The first of these is that there are several genera that are divided by a difference and the negation of that difference, without having any other contrary difference - as the division of animal into rational and non-rational, where the negation cannot be further divided by other differences - and for this reason the division is cut short and terminated before it reaches the most specific species.

The second is that if a genus is divided by two contrary differences, and each of these in the same way by two further contrary ones, and so on down to the ultimate species, the number of species will be even, by the multiplication of a single genus - and if there is a genus that has an odd number of species, it will not fit within this division.

The third is that if one divides the genus of animal by two contrary differences, it will happen that one species of animal falls under both contrary differences - as the division into winged and wingless, under which many of the same species of animal fall, such as the winged and wingless ant; and the division into wild and domestic, under which many of the same species likewise fall.
The fourth is that if one divides a genus by two contrary differences, it will happen that two contrary species fall under each of them, as when animal is divided into aquatic and terrestrial.

And it is known that blooded and bloodless is a major division among the divisions of animal, and each of these differences would be found under each of the aforementioned differences, which is not in keeping with a correct division, since blooded and bloodless both fall under terrestrial and aquatic.
Therefore, because of what has been said above, the division is cut short before it reaches the most specific species.

This will happen when the division is made by natural differences that do not overlap; but if the division is made by accidental, overlapping differences, it will not be cut short, but will instead run to excess, and will not arrive at the natural difference.

But whoever divides a genus by two natural contrary differences, avoiding in the same way everything that is to be avoided in a natural division, will not escape one of these two outcomes: either the division will be cut short before reaching the ultimate species, or, if not, the number of species will not be even.
And these are the reasons why, by dividing, one cannot reach all the most specific species of animal.

And this is why division works in the sciences of arithmetic and geometry, and not in this one: because in this natural science, the composite sensible things are last in the order of discovery, while the simple ones are first in the order of discovery but last in the order of our knowledge - whereas in arithmetic and geometry, matter does not appear in the definitions of things.
And these are the forms by which the species of animal are divided from one another.

For this reason, whoever has not seen or perceived a given species of animal cannot understand or confirm that that species exists, still less understand what it is or of what nature - whereas in arithmetic and geometry, the things that are first in order of discovery are the very same things that are first in our knowledge.

For this reason, all the differences by which a genus is divided in these two sciences are known to us from the outset. This is because matter does not appear in the definitions of the objects of the mathematical sciences, and for this reason it was possible to enumerate the kinds of those two sciences by the method of division.

And perhaps division will still be barred in natural, physical matters, because of the equivocation of the generic name, as in the division of animal into shaped and shapeless - and this does not happen in the mathematical sciences.
It is clear, then, from what has been said, that by the method of division we cannot reach what we intend in this science, and the reason why is apparent.

The method, then, of enumerating the kinds of this science, in an orderly enumeration suited to demonstration, is this: that we first separate animal into genera divided by proportional and corresponding differences - as when we divide animal into blooded and bloodless, since what lacks blood has something proportionate and corresponding to blood.

After this we shall divide the blooded into quadruped, swimming, and flying creatures. And we divide quadruped into the live-bearing and the egg-laying, since these are the differences, proportional and corresponding to one another, that divide the blooded animal - for feathers in the flying creature correspond to scales in fish.
And what has a soft shell corresponds to what has a hard shell.

We are not concerned to divide the genera by more or less, by excess and deficiency - as dividing the flying creature into those with many wings and those with only two - for on this principle we would have to repeat the same things over and over.

Nevertheless, if there is some species that is distinguished by something proper to it that is not found in the whole genus, we shall separate out that species and speak of it apart - as with the ostrich among flying creatures, and the elephant among quadrupeds.

And in general we shall do this for every genus, according to our own sense-perception, or according to our trust in those who have observed - and the endorsement of the masters of this science, for much must be accepted on trust, as with animals we have never seen in our own land. And this is as happens in the science of astronomy, where much has been accepted on trust concerning the mountains of the heavens, trusting those who saw them in their own times.

And in the same way, if we find a species, or several species, distinguished not by more or less - as is the case with man - we shall separate out that species and speak of it apart. This is the method and the way that Aristotle followed in enumerating the kinds of this science; and it appears to be composed of two methods: that of arithmetic and geometry, and that of astronomy - for on the one hand he followed the way of division, and on the other, the way of the senses.

The natural order, then, for presenting this science is this: we begin first by examining what is general and equivocal to every animal, and after this we examine what is general and equivocal to each genus of animal, according to how they are divided by proportional and corresponding differences, and the species of each, which are divided by more and less. After this we shall examine the species known within each genus, by what is proper to each. And this is the ordered way that proceeds from the more general to the more particular.

We shall take care not to repeat the same things too often. We shall proceed in such a way that the demonstrations we make in this work are reckoned from the natural premises already established. This method is composed of two approaches, since the primary genera are divided by differences that are various, proportional, and corresponding, and since these differences are known to us first - for this reason it was fitting to enumerate them by the method of division, and in this respect the work resembles that of arithmetic and geometry.

And since the species that are divided within each genus by what is proper to them are not known to us first, it was necessary to enumerate them by sense, or by the perception of those who observed them - as the master of astronomy did with the motions of the heavens.

Aristotle followed this method in the first ten books of this work, and enumerated the properties of the species of animal that are found among the various genera by their proportional differences; and he set down the properties of the organs that he himself observed, and that he heard from those he had reason to trust, so that no one after him could discover anything beyond what he himself said, except a few things concerning anatomy, which became fully known in the time of Galen.

And we shall state, in their proper places, what Galen discovered beyond Aristotle, citing Galen by name; and we shall record where Aristotle and Galen disagreed as to the usefulness of the organs, and we shall establish the truth of these matters by dialectical reasoning - but as to where they disagreed on points of anatomy, we cannot know this in our own time. These are the matters that Aristotle discussed in this book.
After this let us speak in confirmation of this science, and of what proportion there is between things generable and corruptible and things eternal.

After this we say that our judgment and knowledge concerning generable and corruptible things is greater, more certain, and easier; whereas our judgment and knowledge concerning incorruptible and eternal things is lesser and more difficult. Yet although what we know of these latter is little and hard-won, it is not fitting that we turn away from, or grow distant from, the inquiry into them, since the desire and love of knowing them is greater, and more intensely delightful, and the little we know of them is more precious than the great deal we know of these lower things that are before us.

And this is characteristic of a lover, who values a small thing belonging to the beloved, however slight, more than a great deal of things he does not love, however abundant - and for this reason the proverb arose: 'a little of what is loved is much.'

And the reason why the science of generable and corruptible things is easy, while that of eternal things is difficult and demanding, is that generated and corrupted things are found with us, and within ourselves, and we ourselves are generated through them; whereas eternal things are separated from us in place and in sense-perception. And moreover, the principles we have for knowing them are few, and we acquire them from things that resemble and represent them, and that belong to their kind.

After this, Aristotle admonishes and instructs that whoever undertakes this natural science should not disdain to speak of everything observed concerning the species of animals, but should strive, with all his powers, to speak of all of them, however lowly those species may be.

For many men say that speaking of lowly species is superfluous and idle. Those who say this are mistaken, since the skill and subtlety of nature shine forth more brightly in humble matter, since generation in humble matter is more difficult. This appears also in artificial things: for the sharpness of a craftsman shows more clearly when working with scant, resistant material than with material that is abundant and easily worked.

And so, in general, one must speak of every animal, whether humble or noble, since each partakes, in its own way, of the divine nature we see mingled with it - and we should not be concerned with whether it is humble or noble.

And these are the summaries of what has been said in this book, according to the understanding granted to us by God, though our time for this has been limited, and we have never found a commentary on these books, nor any exposition of them.

And the words of Aristotle are difficult to understand, especially since all the books of this volume are corrupted, and above all the copy I had at hand while composing this summary. Yet, God willing, I shall return again to the words of Aristotle, and correct and set them in order, for this book is exceedingly useful.
Here ends the eleventh.

Averroes said that, since Aristotle enumerated, in the first ten books of this volume, the homogeneous organs, and the heterogeneous ones composed from them, out of which the animal's body is formed, and since in the preceding book, the eleventh, he treated of the dialectical procedures necessary for the master of this science, he wished to speak in this twelfth book, and in the two that follow, so as to show the formal and final causes in each organ of the animal - that is, to show the uses of the organs. And to this he prefixes a certain preliminary discussion needed to establish what he intends.

We say that the modes of composition found in things are three: the first is composition from the four elements - earth, water, air, and fire - which, through the interplay of their qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry), form the matter of composite bodies. Other properties assist these, such as heaviness, lightness, rarity and density, roughness and smoothness, and the like, which bodies also possess.

The second is composition from those things that naturally have parts alike to one another, such as flesh and bone. This kind of composition is treated in general in the fourth book of the Meteorology.
The third is composition from organs that have unlike parts, such as hands and feet.

It is clear that the relation of these compositions to what is composed from them is like the relation of matter to form, and of the antecedent to its completion - for what is prior in these, in nature, is posterior in generation, just as bricks and stones are found only for the sake of a house, not the house for the sake of the stones; so it is in natural things as well.
And it is clear that what is later in time, in both artificial and natural things, is first in definition and in substance.
This is because everything generated is generated from something.
And its generation occurs by a form present in something, and by something that acts as mover, and toward something, which is the end.
And what is generated is generated from something - that is, from some matter - and by its generative agent - that is, a mover - and into something - that is, some form.
And these are one in species, for man generates man, and a tree generates a tree, proceeding from the first to the first.
Therefore, since this is so, matter is first in time, but form is first in finality and in causation.
This is apparent from definition.

For in a definition, the form of anything comes first: hence whoever wishes to define a building - that is, matter together with its mover - cannot avoid including the house itself in that definition; but whoever wishes to define a house need not include the building process, since in the definition of matter, form appears, but in the definition of form, matter does not appear. Since this is so, it is clear that the elements are matter for the organs that have like parts, and that the like parts are matter for the organs that have unlike parts, in which lies the completion and the end of generation.

After this we take up the support belonging to the third mode of composition. For the completion of several modes of generation occurs together in many things; and such is the composition of animals from all these organs - yet any organ made of like parts exists only for the sake of the organ of unlike parts, since operations belong only to these latter organs, such as the hand, the eye, the foot, and the nose.

And since the motions and operations of animals are various, it is fitting that the organic parts be various in form; and since one and the same one of these organs performs various functions, it is likewise fitting that it be composed of several parts of like substance, so that it may have more than one power, since a part of like substance has only one power.

For this reason the hand, which is composed of flesh, sinews, and bones, curves around objects because of the softness of the flesh, grips them because of the sinews, and supports and lifts them because of the hardness of the bones. And for this reason the parts of like substance are many and of various powers, so that one of them is soft, another hard, another moist, another dry, another viscous, and so on, in opposite pairs.

It is clear, then, that if an animal is disposed to perform various operations, it will necessarily be composed of organic parts, and the organic parts of parts of like substance, and the parts of like substance from the elements. It appears, then, from this, that the simple parts exist for the sake of the organic ones, and the organic ones for the sake of the operations.

Then proper ends are found, within the animal, in the parts of like substance, since the animal is composed of these; and these ends are the proper affections of the animal, since, just as the organic parts exist for the sake of actions, so the simple or like parts exist for the sake of affections. For this reason the ancients said that the powers of the five senses are not numbered according to simple parts of like substance, and they said that some of these are attributed to water, some to fire, some to earth, some to air.

This is because the senses are passive powers, not active ones. He means that they are not brought to completion except through external sensible objects, and only then do they pass into act; before this they exist only in potentiality. And although the proper affections of the animal are completed only through the simple parts, some of these parts are also part of some organic whole - otherwise the affection would not be completed, as with the frozen moisture of the eye, which is the seat of sight: the affection of sight would not be perfected unless it were part of the eye. In some cases this is not necessary, as with the flesh, which is the seat of touch, according to Aristotle's view - but whether, among all the operations, there is some operation performed by a part of like substance alone, requires further investigation.

For some hold that certain of the operations of plants are performed by parts of like substance, since the organic parts in plants are hidden and not apparent. And they also hold that some of the internal organs are generated from a single substance, and differ only in shape. It is clear, then, from what has been said, what the usefulness is of organic parts in general, and of parts of like substance.
After this it is fitting that we return to speaking of the usefulness of each organ individually and in particular. And we shall begin first with flesh, following Aristotle's order.
On flesh
We shall undertake first to discover the usefulness of flesh.

It is clear that this part is common to all animals, for in every animal either flesh is found, or something in its place. And it is held, for this reason, that this is the part by which an animal is recognized as such.

We say, then, that the definition of animal is this: an animal is a nourishable body, capable of the sense of touch; and since no animal is found without this sense, it is necessary that in every animal there be found an organ capable of receiving this affection.

And in the same way it is necessary that this sense be present throughout the whole body of the animal, since it is not found only in some particular part, as the other senses are; and this is because an animal is not an animal except by this sense of touch. And an animal is such throughout its whole body, not in some one part; and this is a part common to the whole body of the animal.

And it must be simple, of like parts, since a simple sense operates through a simple organ, and a composite sense through a composite organ. And since the powers of the five senses are passive, it is necessary that the organs of these senses be of like parts, since organs of this kind have no active power, but only receive what comes to them from external sensible things.

And it is fitting that one power correspond to one organ, since only one form is found in one matter; and this is how it is found in the five senses, since each of the five senses is found first in an organ of like parts - as the sense of sight, which is found first in the frozen moisture of the eye, and the sense of hearing in the air contained within the ear. But since in each organ of the four remaining senses a composite sense is found - that is, a sense proper to that organ, and the common sense, which is the sense of touch - it is necessary that these organs be composite.

And since the sense of touch is simple and not composite, it must operate through a simple organ; and since no such organ is found in the animal except flesh, or what stands in its place, it necessarily follows that flesh is the proper organ of the sense of touch, so that its relation to what is sensed by touch is like the relation of the frozen moisture to what is sensed by sight - and this organ is the first simple body of the animal. For this reason, in every animal either flesh is found, or something in its place. And it would follow from this that an animal in which only the sense of touch is found has only this one organ - that is, flesh, or what stands in its place - as is the case with sea shellfish. And Galen cannot deny this, although he himself said that it is the sinews that cause flesh to feel. For it makes no difference, as we have explained, whether touch is found in the flesh itself or because of the sinews.

For it is clear that flesh feels in every part of itself; and moreover, as Galen himself says, sinew is slow to feel - and for this reason we cannot say that an animal feels only because of the sinews.

And Galen appears to hold the same view regarding the sense of sight. For he himself says that sight is due to the two hollow optic nerves, and yet he also says that the crystalline moisture is the proper organ of sight. And this would be true if it were assumed that sinews are found in every animal; but if they are not found in every animal, then their only role in the sense would be to make the sense better in the animal that has sinews. It appears, then, from what has been said, what the usefulness of flesh is, and that it is the proper organ of the sense of touch.

And since it is necessary that in every animal a common action be found, just as a common affection is found, it is necessary that there be found in it an organ for this action - namely, of nourishment and of motion. For this reason there must be found an organic part, and this action occurs only through an organic part common to the whole animal, and this part is the heart. Just as the simple common part, which is flesh, is found, so too, since the heart is the principle of sensation, it must be fleshly; and since it is the principle of the animal's common action, it must necessarily be organic.
And Aristotle says that the organ that is the principle of nourishment, of sensation, and of motion must be a single organ in the animal.
Galen concedes this for sensation and motion, but not for nourishment.
Aristotle says that the organ in which these three powers are gathered together is the heart.
Galen says that the power of nourishment is in the liver, and the power of sensation and motion in the brain.

We shall investigate this matter as best we can. What we have said - that the heart must be fleshly, since it is the principle of the sense of touch - holds only if it is assumed that flesh is the first and proper organ of touch; for from what has been said it is not clear that flesh is the first organ, but only that it is the proper one. For if we assumed that flesh is the first organ, we would fall into one of two difficulties: either the animal would exist without sinew and brain, or sinew and brain would be excluded from the sense of touch altogether.
But this would be a manifest falsehood, for it is clear from anatomy that the brain and the sinews, in an animal that has them, do participate in the sense of touch.

It is clear, then, from this, that either the sense of touch is greater and better because of the sinews and the brain, or else sinew and brain will be found in every animal. And if we suppose that this sense exists because of the sinews and the brain, it is not clear which of these is true, from the mere fact that sinew and brain enliven the sense of touch in an animal that has them. And since it is not apparent from anatomy that every animal has sinews and a brain, this remains a matter of doubt.
For it appears that shellfish either lack sinews and a brain, or that these are too hidden within them to detect.

Therefore, since this is so, we must hold to the word of Aristotle, from which it appears that flesh is the first organ, and the proper organ, of the sense of touch; and that it is the proper organ is made clear by our complete explanation above, and that it is the first is shown by Aristotle's own statement, who held that the power of a simple sense is one, belonging to one power, and that a single power has a single, simple organ - just as a composite power has a composite organ. And given this, it is clear that sinew and brain are found in an animal that has them only so that the sense may be greater and better in it, since such an animal has a greater heat, which the sinews and brain temper; and the sense of touch exists only through the tempering and balance of the four qualities.

And Galen agrees with this, for he says that the skin of the palm and of the tip of the index finger have the best sense of touch, since they possess a greater temperance and better balance than other parts of the body; yet he contradicts himself, for he says that the brain is cold and moist, and the sinews cold and dry, and also says that it was the principle of the sense of touch.
Therefore, according to all this, it must necessarily be that flesh is the primary organ of the sense of touch.

For it is agreed by all that flesh is the most temperate part of the whole body, and that the sense of touch must operate through a temperate organ. It appears, then, from what has been said, that flesh is the first and proper organ of the sense of touch, and that the heart is the principle of this power - that is, of touch - and this neither helps nor harms Aristotle's statement, as was shown in the anatomical findings of Galen and others after Aristotle.
How admirable, then, is the divine power at work in the words of this man! Truly, they are far removed from excess.

And what Galen supposed concerning the sinews and the brain - that they are necessary for sensation, because he observed this in some animal - is of the same kind as what he supposed concerning the gallbladder and the spleen, that they are found in every nourishable animal, merely because he found them in certain animals.

And it is not hidden from a student of this science that actions common to every animal may, in some particular animal, be performed by several organs together. And this will be either so that the action is better performed in that animal, or because of some incidental feature of that particular animal. And this end belongs among the ends of flesh.

What we have explained up to this point is the first end and the first act, according to nature's intention; and the other ends that Galen attributes to flesh, if they are indeed ends, are so only through a secondary act. And once this is established concerning flesh, it will become apparent that the other bodies of like substance found in the animal exist only for one of two reasons: either for the advantage or the needs of the flesh, as bone for support and blood for nourishment, or as a necessary consequence of the generation of flesh itself, such as the dry and moist residues of excretion.

And it is possible that both of these are found together in some substances - that is, the necessity of advantage and the necessity of consequence - as in suet, marrow, bile, and black bile. And he speaks properly here of those things that are generated together with the animal.

And afterward he will speak of the others, when he comes to speak of the generation of the animal. And since it is fitting, for one intending to show the effects and advantages of a thing, that he first set forth its nature, and since a nature cannot be verified unless one first shows what elements it is composed of, it is necessary to set forth beforehand the hot and the cold, the moist and the dry, and how each of these is defined, and what the effects of these qualities are. For this is the proper approach.

And since the ancients were ignorant of this, they were divided by various opinions in natural matters, with great disagreement - as, for instance, over which is hotter, the male or the female, in land and water animals.
And for this reason Aristotle rebukes them, saying: 'If they disagree about matters close at hand, how much more will they disagree about what is hidden and remote?'
And Aristotle spoke rightly of these two qualities above the others, since they are the cause of life and death, of youth and old age, of sleep and waking, and of the other things found in an animal.
And the method here is to enumerate the effects by which these qualities are made apparent in things.
And so we call hot everything in which greater heat is found, and the heat of one who touches it is increased by the touching of it.
And we call hot that which we find has a strong effect on the sense.
And we call hot that with which, when something is mixed, that thing becomes hot to the sense of touch.
And this is what is called hot in potentiality, as foods and spices are.
And we call hot whatever melts and burns.
And we say that, of two things equal in quality, the one greater in quantity is hotter.
Thanks be to God. Amen.
